Holding otherwise would reward officials who hide public assets abroad. A New York court had itself deferred to Philippine courts out of comity.

arelma.vote: 5–0, Sereno, C.J. (Special Second Division). Brion, J., sat in place of Carpio, J., who took no part. No separate opinions.

iss.q: Do the petitions present a political question beyond the Court’s power?
iss.why: EDSA I was extra-constitutional: it overthrew the whole government, and the legitimacy of the government it produced was beyond review (Lawyers League v. Aquino). EDSA II was intra-constitutional: an exercise of speech and assembly that affected only the Office of the President; Arroyo took her oath under the 1987 Constitution. The issues (Art. VII, Secs. 8 and 11, immunity) are legal.

iss.q: Did Estrada resign as President on January 20, 2001?
iss.why: Resignation is a question of fact: intent to resign plus acts of relinquishment, in any form. The Angara Diary shows he proposed a snap election he would not run in, negotiated only the terms of his exit, and said “Ayoko na”; his farewell statement acknowledged Arroyo’s oath and left “for the sake of peace.” RA 3019, Sec. 12 (no resignation while a case is pending) did not bar it: it aims to stop resignation as a shield, the Ombudsman cases were not pending against a sitting President, and the impeachment had collapsed.

iss.q: Is Estrada only temporarily unable to act, making Arroyo merely Acting President?
iss.why: Sec. 11 commits the question of inability to Congress. Both Houses recognized Arroyo as President (House Res. Nos. 175, 176 and 178; Senate Res. Nos. 82, 83 and 84; laws sent to her for signature; her nominee confirmed as Vice-President). That decision of a co-equal branch is a political question the Court cannot revise.

iss.q: Must Estrada be convicted by the Senate before he can be prosecuted, and is he immune from suit?
iss.why: The impeachment court was declared functus officio; requiring conviction first would make him better off than a President never impeached. Immunity lasts only during tenure (In re Bermudez); the 1987 Constitution did not reenact the 1981 amendment’s post-tenure immunity. Plunder, bribery and graft are not covered: public office is a public trust.

iss.q: Should the Ombudsman’s investigation be stopped because of prejudicial publicity?
iss.why: Pervasive publicity is not prejudicial per se. Under the actual prejudice test (Martelino; Webb), he must prove that the investigators were actually influenced, not that they might be; he offered news reports and no proof of the panel’s bias.

estradaarroyo.vote: 11–0 in the result, Puno, J. Buena, Kapunan, Pardo, Ynares-Santiago and Sandoval-Gutierrez, JJ., concurred in the result (Pardo, J.: Estrada “was constrained to resign”; he reserved his vote on immunity). Davide, C.J. and Panganiban, J., took no part.
estradaarroyo.ops: Panganiban, J. explained his inhibition (not a vote on the merits): inhibition is voluntary and discretionary, and he stepped aside so that no one could doubt the integrity of the proceedings. Davide, C.J.’s explanation and the reserved separate opinions are not in the files.

iss.q: Does Sec. 12 impose a ministerial duty to release the President’s medical records, enforceable by mandamus?
iss.why: Mandamus needs a well-defined, clear and certain right and a ministerial duty. The framers left it to the Office of the President “to choose the appropriate means of releasing information,” and the President’s condition “to the President and his doctor” (Commissioner Ople). The petition failed to show a prima facie case, so it was dismissed outright.

iss.q: Did the petitioner show a serious illness that triggers Sec. 12?
iss.why: The claimed illnesses rested on online news articles, hearsay twice removed (Lagman v. Medialdea), while the President was visibly holding regular Cabinet meetings and televised addresses on the pandemic. The claim was surmise and conjecture.

iss.q: Does the right to information (Art. III, Sec. 7) entitle the petitioner to the records, or to new examinations?
iss.why: Having found no clear legal right under Sec. 12, the Court found it unnecessary to address the other issues.

deleon.vote: Unsigned Resolution, May 8, 2020. Leonen and Caguioa, JJ., dissented (opinions not in the files).

iss.q: Does Art. VII, Sec. 13 admit the broad exceptions for appointive officials in Art. IX-B, Sec. 7(2), so that EO 284 is valid?
iss.why: The framers wrote a separate provision for the President’s official family to impose a stricter rule, after the Marcos-era practice of Cabinet members sitting on dozens of boards. Sec. 13 is not limited to office “in the Government,” so it covers public and private office. “Unless otherwise provided in this Constitution” means only the Constitution’s own exceptions: the VP as Cabinet member, the VP acting as President, and the Secretary of Justice on the JBC. Reading Art. IX-B into it would erase the distinction. EO 284, which allows two more offices, is void.

iss.q: Does the prohibition cover posts held ex officio, without additional compensation, as provided by law and as required by primary functions?
iss.why: Such posts are additional duties of the principal office, not “any other office”; otherwise the President could not chair the National Security Council and the Finance Secretary could not sit on the Monetary Board. The duty must be required, not merely allowed, by the primary functions; posts that are incidental or alien to them, or that carry management functions or pay (GOCC chairmanships, directorships), are not covered. No extra compensation may be received, by whatever name.

iss.q: Must the officials give up the other posts and refund what they received?
iss.why: Five Secretaries still holding other offices were ordered to give them up immediately; the petitions were moot as to the rest. As de facto officers who served in good faith, they may keep the per diems and allowances received for actual services (Castillo v. Arrieta).

clu.vote: 13–0, Fernan, C.J. Sarmiento and Griño-Aquino, JJ., took no part.
clu.ops: Paras, J., concurring: “cabinet members like the members of the Supreme Court are not supermen.”

iss.q: Did the COA gravely abuse its discretion in disallowing the per diems and allowances paid to the alternates of Cabinet members on the NHA Board?
iss.why: PD 757 names the Secretaries as the Board members; the petitioners sat only as their alternates, whose acts are the acts of their principals. Under Civil Liberties Union, Secretaries sitting ex officio may receive no extra compensation by whatever name, because the ex officio post is part of their principal office. The alternates cannot have a better right than their principals, so PD 757’s “right to receive their benefit” is limited to what the principals may lawfully receive.

cruzcoa.vote: 13–0, Sandoval-Gutierrez, J. Quisumbing, J. (a former Labor Secretary) took no part; Buena, J., on official leave. No separate opinions.

iss.q: Is the COA memorandum enforcing the ban void for lack of publication?
iss.why: It is an internal, interpretative letter of instruction to COA auditors to enforce the self-executing Art. VII, Sec. 13, not a rule implementing a statute, so Tañada v. Tuvera does not require publication. Civil Liberties Union had already explained the prohibition, and the Court’s interpretation is part of the law.

iss.q: Are the representatives of the ex officio members, all below Assistant Secretary, covered by the prohibitions on multiple offices and additional compensation?
iss.why: Art. IX-B, Sec. 7(2): no law or order created a position for them or authorized extra pay, and they were merely designated, not appointed; designation carries no salary (Dimaandal v. COA). Art. VII, Sec. 13: their principals cannot receive per diems or honoraria under Civil Liberties Union, and the representative cannot have a better right than his principal (Dela Cruz v. COA; Bitonio v. COA).

iss.q: Could the COA reopen accounts already settled?
iss.why: PD 1445, Sec. 52 allows the COA to open and revise settled accounts within three years. The Government is not estopped by its agents’ mistakes.

iss.q: Is the NAC administrative order’s clause on the representatives’ pay void, as the COA ruled?
iss.why: On its face it makes pay subject to what is “authorized by law,” and the law prohibits it; the error lay in how it was read. Representatives may attend only as guests or witnesses; they cannot take the ex officio members’ place in determining a quorum, deliberating or deciding.

iss.q: Are the representatives de facto officers who may keep the allowances?
iss.why: A de facto officer holds under a colorable appointment; designees have none. They also cannot claim good faith after Civil Liberties Union became final and the prohibition was express.

nacoa.vote: 12–0, Corona, J. Austria-Martinez and Carpio Morales, JJ., on official leave. No separate opinions.

iss.q: Is the President’s decision to bar the Marcoses a political question beyond the Court’s power?
iss.why: Art. VIII, Sec. 1 lets the Court determine grave abuse of discretion by any branch, so the doctrine is narrowed. But review is limited: the Court checks, it does not supplant, the Executive (Lansang v. Garcia).

iss.q: Is the right involved the right to travel and liberty of abode (Art. III, Sec. 6)?
iss.why: It is the right to return to one’s country, distinct under the UDHR (Art. 13(2)) and the ICCPR (Art. 12(4): no one may be arbitrarily deprived of it). It is not in the Bill of Rights but is part of the law of the land as a generally accepted principle of international law (Art. II, Sec. 2). The limits on travel and abode do not govern it.

iss.q: May the President, under the Constitution, bar the Marcoses from returning?
iss.why: Art. VII, Sec. 1 vests “the executive power” without defining it; the list of specific powers does not exhaust it. The President is head of state and of government, and the 1987 Constitution, while limiting specific powers, keeps intact what is traditionally executive power. Her residual power to protect the general welfare (Art. II, Secs. 4 and 5), as protector of the peace, covers day-to-day peace and order short of the Commander-in-Chief powers. Even the House resolution appealed to her compassion, not her power.

iss.q: Did the President act arbitrarily or with grave abuse of discretion in finding that the return threatened the national interest?
iss.why: Factual bases existed: the insurgency, secessionists, rightist plots and the Marcoses’ documented efforts to destabilize the government; their return could be the “final straw.” The State may act pre-emptively against nascent threats, and the economic risk was within judicial notice.

manglapus.vote: Dismissed, Cortes, J. Concurring as printed: Narvasa, Melencio-Herrera, Gancayco, Griño-Aquino, Medialdea and Regalado, JJ. Dissenting: Gutierrez, Jr. (joined by Bidin), Sarmiento, Padilla, Cruz and Paras, JJ. Feliciano, J., on leave. Later cases call it 8–7.
manglapus.ops: Gutierrez, Jr., J.: a question of rights, not power; liberty of abode yields only to a court and travel only to a law, and none exists; the “catalytic effect” is speculation. Sarmiento, J.: the 1987 Constitution took the President “out of the picture”; there is no getting even in a democracy. Padilla, J.: police power may limit travel even without a law, but not arbitrarily, and the threat was not shown; Ninoy had the same right in 1983. Cruz, J.: the government “failed dismally” to prove its case; residual powers are “a great leap backward.” Paras, J.: let him return under house arrest in Ilocos Norte.

iss.q: Should the Court relax the procedural defects and allow certiorari despite the lapse of the period to appeal?
iss.why: Rules serve, not override, substantial justice. Given the public interest, the need for stability in the public service and the effect on the executive department, the Court reached the merits; executing the RTC decision would be an oppressive exercise of judicial authority.

iss.q: May the DENR Secretary reorganize the department by moving the Region XII offices from Cotabato City to Koronadal?
iss.why: Under qualified political agency (Joson v. Torres), a corollary of the control power (Art. VII, Sec. 17), the Secretary’s acts are presumptively the President’s unless disapproved. The President’s continuing power to reorganize (Administrative Code, Book III, Sec. 20; PD 1416 as amended) may be delegated to the Secretary (DOTC v. Mabalot). The RTC should have taken judicial notice of RA 6734 and EO 429, which made Koronadal the regional center; the power to reorganize regions includes fixing their centers (Chiongbian v. Orbos).

iss.q: May the courts stop the transfer as untimely or unwise?
iss.why: No buildings yet, Ramadan, schooling and the lack of consultation go to wisdom, not legality. Without a constitutional infirmity or grave abuse, the courts will not oversee the bureaucracy.

denr12.vote: 4–0, Ynares-Santiago, J. (First Division). Davide, C.J., abroad on official business. No separate opinions.

iss.q: Does the petition qualify as a class suit?
iss.why: Designating a case a class suit does not make it one (Rule 3, Sec. 12). The petition did not state how many employees were affected (about 549); only 20 of the 67 signatories subscribed before the notary, 32 desisted, and the employees’ association opposed the suit, showing a divergence of interests. The Court nonetheless ruled on the merits.

iss.q: Could President Arroyo amend EO 285, a law issued by President Aquino with legislative powers, through EO 378?
iss.why: The President may reorganize executive offices under the power of control and under statutes delegating the power to reorganize: the Administrative Code (Book III, Sec. 31, read with the residual powers in Sec. 20) and the appropriations laws (Larin; Buklod ng Kawaning EIIB). The NPO is part of the Office of the President. The express power to abolish, merge and transfer carries the lesser power to modify functions; EO 378 abolished nothing and transferred nothing. The power covers only the Executive, not the Judiciary, Congress or constitutional bodies.

iss.q: Does EO 378 violate the employees’ security of tenure because it is a bad-faith step toward abolishing the NPO?
iss.why: A reorganization in good faith, for economy or efficiency, is valid even if positions are lost; one done for political reasons or to defeat tenure is void (Dario v. Mison). Whoever alleges bad faith must prove it, and the employees showed no position abolished or employee removed, and no political motive.

banda.vote: 14–0, Leonardo-de Castro, J. Abad, J., on official leave.
banda.ops: Carpio, J., concurring in the result: Sec. 31 is a narrow, closed list (restructure the OP Proper; transfer functions or agencies), and the NPO is not part of the OP Proper; PD 1416, on which Larin rests, is an undue delegation that lapsed when Congress convened; control means reviewing a subordinate’s acts, not restructuring offices. EO 378 is valid only because it implements the competitive-bidding policy of RA 9184.

iss.q: Do the petitioners have standing?
iss.why: The Representatives sue to protect the powers of Congress: an injury to Congress injures each member (PHILCONSA v. Enriquez). Biraogo showed no direct injury, but the rule was relaxed for a matter of transcendental importance.

iss.q: Does EO 1 usurp Congress’s power to create public offices and appropriate funds?
iss.why: Not because of the power to reorganize: Administrative Code, Book III, Sec. 31 covers altering existing offices, not creating one. Not because of control: control is the power to alter or set aside a subordinate’s acts, “entirely different from the power to create public offices.” Not because of PD 1416, a transitional delegation that became functus officio when Congress convened. The basis is the faithful-execution clause: the power to investigate, and to create ad hoc bodies to do so, is inherent in the Chief Executive (Marcos v. Manglapus; DOH v. Camposano). Funding from existing OP appropriations is an allotment, not an appropriation.

iss.q: Does the Truth Commission supplant the Ombudsman and the DOJ?
iss.why: It is fact-finding, not quasi-judicial: to investigate is to inquire; to adjudicate is to settle rights finally (Cariño v. CHR). Its findings are recommendatory; probable cause stays with the Ombudsman and the DOJ, whose investigative powers are not exclusive (Ombudsman v. Galicia). It complements them.

iss.q: Does EO 1 violate the equal protection clause?
iss.why: Equal protection binds all state action, including the Executive’s. EO 1 names the “previous administration” three times; that administration is “but just a member of a class” of past administrations. Reports of corruption, the risk of overburden and the freshness of evidence are not substantial distinctions. Underinclusion is not fatal when inadvertent, but here it was deliberate, and Sec. 17 (expansion at the President’s discretion) does not cure it. Reasonable prioritization is allowed; a revised order covering earlier administrations could pass.

iss.q: Are the petitioners entitled to injunctive relief?
iss.why: Not discussed separately; the fallo, “as also prayed for,” ordered the respondents to cease and desist from carrying out EO 1.

biraogo.vote: 10–5, Mendoza, J. With him: Corona, C.J., Velasco, Leonardo-de Castro, Brion, Peralta, Bersamin, Del Castillo, Villarama and Perez, JJ. Dissenting: Carpio (joined by Abad), Carpio Morales and Sereno, JJ.; Nachura, J., concurring and dissenting (dissenting on equal protection).
biraogo.ops: Carpio, J. (joined by Abad, J.): EO 1 is valid in every respect; Sec. 31 includes creating offices in the OP Proper; the focus on the last administration is reasonable (prescription, earlier administrations already investigated, fresher evidence); the ruling gives every administration “a cloak of immunity.” Carpio Morales, J.: equal protection was not properly raised by these petitioners, and the classification rests on period, not personalities. Nachura, J.: the President may create the body under control and the take-care clause; rational basis test met; “previous administration” sets a time frame, not a class. Abad, J.: “you cannot order five men to pull a train that a thousand men cannot move.” Sereno, J.: prioritization is not classification; the ruling defeats public accountability.

iss.q: Is the Philippine Tourism Authority, a GOCC, covered by the Productivity Incentives Act (RA 6971), putting its employees’ 1992 bonus beyond AO 29?
iss.why: The PTA’s functions are mostly governmental, but the test is legislative intent: RA 6971’s provisions on collective bargaining, strikes and the NCMB fit only private firms and GOCCs incorporated under the general corporation law. GOCCs with original charters are under the Civil Service and have their own incentive award system.

iss.q: Are AO 268 and AO 29 valid?
iss.why: They are an exercise of the President’s control over executive departments (Art. VII, Sec. 17): he may alter, modify or set aside a subordinate’s acts and substitute his judgment, motu proprio (Mondano; Lacson-Magallanes). Uneven bonuses caused dissension and conflicted with salary standardization. Bodies with fiscal autonomy (the Judiciary, the CSC, COA, COMELEC, the Ombudsman) are not covered.

iss.q: Did the AOs usurp the Civil Service Commission’s authority over the incentive awards system?
iss.why: They regulated the grant and amount; they did not revoke the privilege. Managing government money is an executive function, and the Administrative Code itself authorizes “the President or the head of each department” to incur the expense.

iss.q: Is the forced refund an impairment of contracts, or the personal liability of the officials who granted the benefits?
iss.why: A bonus is not a demandable obligation, and the acts were governmental. Officials are not personally liable without bad faith; good faith and regularity are presumed.

iss.q: Must the employees refund the 1992 benefits they received?
iss.why: All parties acted in good faith: the officials paid in the honest belief that the benefits were due, and the employees received them believing they deserved them. Further deductions were enjoined.

blaquera.vote: 13–0, Purisima, J. Regalado, J., on official leave. No separate opinions.

iss.q: Is HPPL entitled to an injunction against the rebidding, as the declared winning bidder?
iss.why: Injunction needs a clear and unmistakable right. The SBMA Board and officers are under the control and supervision of the Office of the President, and LOI 620 requires the President’s approval for contracts of ₱2 million and up. The President may, for justifiable reasons, overturn the Board’s award; the discretion to accept or reject bids, or recall an award, is so wide that courts will not interfere unless it shields unfairness. The award was not final, so HPPL had no clear right.

iss.q: Does HPPL, a foreign corporation without a license to do business here, have capacity to sue?
iss.why: Taking part in a bidding is doing business in the Philippines: it exercises the purpose for which the corporation was created (Granger Associates). An unlicensed foreign corporation doing business here cannot sue in Philippine courts.

hutchison.vote: Ynares-Santiago, J. (First Division). Puno, Kapunan and Pardo, JJ., concur; Davide, C.J., concurs in the result. No separate opinions.

iss.q: Did NEA’s early payment of the 1997 salary increases have legal basis?
iss.why: The 1997 GAA is not self-executory: personal services are appropriated in lump sums and need an itemization and expenditure program approved by the President, and no salary increase may be paid without a law or budget circular (Administrative Code, Book IV, Secs. 23 and 34; Book VI, Sec. 60). EO 389’s exception covers only GOCCs without enough funds; the 1995 OP memorandum allowed acceleration only with prior DBM approval, which NEA never got; approval of a proposed budget is not approval to disburse.

iss.q: Did the President lack authority to issue EO 389?
iss.why: Executive orders implement constitutional or statutory powers (Administrative Code, Book III); Joint Resolution No. 01 itself contemplated a governing executive order. And the President’s control over all executive offices (Art. VII, Sec. 17) reaches every employee, is self-executing and cannot be limited by Congress (De Leon v. Carpio); there is only one Chief Executive (Villena), whose directives subordinates must implement in good faith.

iss.q: Did the COA exceed its powers by asking whether NEA violated laws, not just whether an appropriation existed?
iss.why: Guevara v. Gimenez was decided under the 1935 Constitution and is no longer controlling (Caltex v. COA). Under Art. IX-D, Sec. 2, the COA audits all accounts, including GOCCs’, and may disallow irregular or illegal expenditures. It properly read RA 8244 and EO 389 together.

iss.q: Do standing, mootness or prematurity bar the petition?
iss.why: The intervention of the president of the League of Provinces made standing academic; mootness was not raised and was deemed waived. On prematurity (raised only by the dissent), an act seriously alleged to violate the Constitution ripens into a controversy upon its issuance (Tañada v. Angara).

iss.q: Is Sec. 1 of AO 372, “directing” LGUs to cut spending by 25%, a valid exercise of general supervision?
iss.why: Supervision is oversight: seeing that subordinates perform their duties, without laying down or replacing the rules (Mondano; Drilon v. Lim). LGUs enjoy fiscal autonomy, and Sec. 284’s conditions were not met. The Court accepted the Solicitor General’s assurance that Sec. 1 is only an advisory, so no sanction may be imposed on LGUs that do not follow it.

iss.q: Is Sec. 4, withholding 10% of the LGUs’ internal revenue allotment, valid?
iss.why: The just share “shall be automatically released” (Art. X, Sec. 6) and “shall not be subject to any lien or holdback … for whatever purpose” (LGC Sec. 286). A holdback is something withheld, often temporarily, so the temporary nature does not matter. The President may adjust the IRA only under Sec. 284, and the government showed no unmanageable deficit and no consultation with the leagues. Laudable purposes must be pursued by legal means.

pimentelaguirre.vote: 12–3, Panganiban, J. Kapunan, J., dissented, joined by Purisima and Ynares-Santiago, JJ.
pimentelaguirre.ops: Kapunan, J., dissenting: the case was premature, since the withholding was temporary and no refusal to release was shown. The President, as chief fiscal officer, may withhold temporarily: the power to reduce the IRA in a deficit (Sec. 284) includes the lesser power to hold it back until the fiscal picture is known. “No lien or holdback” is not in the Constitution, and consultation is presumed.

iss.q: Must a person first admit committing the offense before invoking the amnesty proclamation?
iss.why: The Commission’s view rested on a wrong idea of amnesty. Pardon is private, granted after conviction, and forgives the punishment; under RPC Art. 36 it does not restore political rights unless it says so, nor remit civil indemnity. Amnesty is a public act of which courts take judicial notice, granted to classes of political offenders, and it obliterates the offense: the person stands as though he committed none. So it applies whether pleaded or not, whenever the evidence of either side shows the act falls within the proclamation. Motive may be inferred from witnesses, not only from the accused. Requiring a confession would defeat the proclamation, since few would risk it. And the right, once shown, cannot be waived: the law regards such persons as patriots, not criminals.

iss.q: Does mandamus lie to compel the Commission to hear and decide the applications?
iss.why: The Commission returned the cases without deciding whether the petitioners were entitled to amnesty, on the wrong premise that an admission was needed, so it had not done the duty the proclamation and AO No. 11 imposed. It must hold a summary hearing if needed and decide.

barrioquinto.vote: 6–2, Feria, J. Perfecto, J., concurring; Tuason, J., dissenting, joined by Pablo, J.
barrioquinto.ops: Perfecto, J., concurring: only three elements are needed for a hearing (an RPC offense not against chastity or for personal motives; in furtherance of the resistance; within the period); nothing in the proclamation requires an admission. Tuason, J., dissenting: the Commission did hear and decide, and mandamus cannot control its discretion; “amnesty presupposes the commission of a crime,” so it is a “rank inconsistency” to seek forgiveness for an act one denies. The dissent’s view became the law in Llanita, Guillermo and Vera.

iss.q: Must a person invoking Amnesty Proclamation No. 8 first admit having committed the crime?
iss.why: Barrioquinto, De Los Santos and Viray were superseded and deemed overruled by People v. Llanita and People v. Guillermo (1950): it is a “rank inconsistency” to seek forgiveness for an act one claims not to have committed; amnesty presupposes a crime; invoking it is a plea of confession and avoidance; and where the proclamation imposes conditions, the accused must prove them. Buyco v. People reiterates it. None of the petitioners admitted the killing, so the Commission could not take cognizance.

iss.q: Do the facts bring the killing within Proclamation No. 8?
iss.why: “At any rate,” the killing was due to rivalry between the Hunters guerrillas and Vera’s guerrillas, not in furtherance of the resistance or against a person aiding the enemy.

iss.q: Did the CA err in applying DOJ Administrative Order No. 144 (1950)?
iss.why: The order, requiring the accused to claim that he committed the acts in furtherance of the resistance, was issued precisely under Llanita and Guillermo.

iss.q: Did the CA err in declining to resolve the factual issues (that the victim aided the enemy)?
iss.why: A ruling would be premature, prejudicial and useless, because the case came from a body without jurisdiction; jurisdiction may be raised at any stage.

iss.q: Did the absolute pardon restore Santos’s right to vote despite the Election Code’s disqualification of persons convicted of crimes against property?
iss.why: The pardoning power has only two constitutional limits: it is exercised after conviction, and not in impeachment cases; subject to those, “the pardoning power cannot be restricted or controlled by legislative action.” An absolute pardon blots out the crime and removes all disabilities resulting from the conviction, accessory and resultant alike. The voting ban rests on the conviction, so the pardon reaches it; granted after the sentence was served, it removes all that is left of the conviction’s consequences. Otherwise only Congress could restore the right, an impairment the Constitution did not contemplate.

iss.q: Was the pardon absolute as to Santos’s political rights despite its condition on public office?
iss.why: It is conditional only in limiting him to clerical or manual posts; it is absolute insofar as it restores “full civil and political rights,” including suffrage.

cristobal.vote: 4–1, Laurel, J. Avanceña, C.J., Imperial and Diaz, JJ., concur; Horrilleno, J., dissents.
cristobal.ops: Horrilleno, J., dissenting: the pardon had no object, since the sentence and its accessories had been served; a pardon “involves forgiveness and not forgetfulness” and does not erase the conviction or the moral stain; and the voting ban is not a penalty but a police measure based on character, which the Legislature alone may fix (suffrage belongs to those “not otherwise disqualified by law”). The office limit made the pardon conditional, not absolute.

iss.q: Is a final conviction for a new crime necessary before a conditionally pardoned convict can be rearrested and recommitted for breaching the pardon?
iss.why: Tesoro, Sales and Espuelas settled it: (1) granting a pardon and fixing its conditions are purely executive acts; (2) the breach and its consequences may be determined by the President under Sec. 64(i) of the Revised Administrative Code (no judicial pronouncement needed) or by a court under RPC Art. 159; Art. 159 did not repeal Sec. 64(i); (3) the choice is the President’s prerogative. Here the President chose Sec. 64(i). The issue is only whether the convict broke his undertaking, for purposes of reimposing the remitted sentence; punishing the new crimes still needs final convictions.

iss.q: Was Torres denied due process because he was not heard before his arrest and recommitment?
iss.why: Due process is not “semper et ubique” judicial process. He was tried and convicted of the original offense with full judicial process, and by accepting the pardon he agreed that the Executive would determine whether its condition was broken, a determination conclusive on him (Sales, quoting Fuller v. Alabama; Espuelas).

torresgonzales.vote: 10–2, Feliciano, J. Cruz, J., dissenting, joined by Paras, J. Yap, J., on leave; Narvasa, J., took no part.
torresgonzales.ops: Cruz, J., dissenting (joined by Paras, J.): mere accusation is not guilt; “it is the conviction that makes him a criminal,” and only a judge convicts. Sec. 64(i) is valid for non-criminal conditions, but letting the President decide whether a crime was committed encroaches on judicial power. A conditional pardon is a contract that binds the State too and must be construed in the grantee’s favor. He would reverse Espuelas and order Torres released.

iss.q: Did the pardon, granted while her appeal was pending, operate as an acquittal so that the usual rules on pardon do not apply?
iss.why: The 1981 amendment to the 1973 Constitution had dropped the final-conviction requirement (the 1987 Constitution restored it), so a pardon pending appeal was possible. Either way, by accepting it she abandoned her appeal and the conviction became final. A pardon is an act of grace exempting one from the punishment for a crime he has committed (U.S. v. Wilson), not a finding of innocence.

iss.q: Is a pardoned officer entitled to reinstatement to her former post without a new appointment?
iss.why: Philippine cases (Cristobal; Pelobello) followed Ex parte Garland’s view that a pardon makes the offender “a new man.” The Court adopted the more realistic modern view: pardon implies guilt and relieves the offender of the punitive consequences of the crime, including disqualifications, “but it relieves him from nothing more.” It removed her disqualification from public employment, so she may apply again, but it does not restore a forfeited office; the appointing power may weigh the facts of the offense, since public office is for the common good.

iss.q: Is she entitled to backpay for the period of her suspension?
iss.why: A pardon looks to the future and is not retrospective; what was suffered under a judicially established conviction is presumed rightly suffered, and the government owes no reparation.

iss.q: Does the pardon exempt her from the civil indemnity imposed by the sentence?
iss.why: RPC Art. 36: a pardon “shall in no case exempt the culprit from the payment of the civil indemnity.” Civil liability ex delicto survives pardon and is extinguished only by the Civil Code modes (payment, remission, compensation and the like).

monsanto.vote: 15–0, Fernan, C.J. Nine concurred fully; Melencio-Herrera, Padilla, Feliciano, Gutierrez, Cruz and Sarmiento, JJ., concurred in the result.
monsanto.ops: Padilla, J. (joined by Melencio-Herrera and Sarmiento, JJ.): the pardon extinguished criminal liability, but under RPC Art. 36 it restores the right to hold office or vote only if it says so expressly; “full civil and political rights” is not enough, and Cristobal and Pelobello should be modified. Feliciano, J. (joined by Melencio-Herrera, Gutierrez, Cruz and Sarmiento, JJ.): Arts. 36 and 40–43 require explicitness “in printer’s ink”; they are not an unconstitutional limit on the pardoning power, only a requirement that the President be clear.

iss.q: Did the COMELEC gravely abuse its discretion in ruling that Estrada’s pardon made him qualified to vote and be voted for?
iss.why: (1) The pardoning power has only constitutional limits: impeachment, no final conviction, and election offenses without the COMELEC’s recommendation; Congress cannot restrict it (Cristobal; Pelobello; Monsanto), and the framers rejected a clause allowing that. (2) RPC Arts. 36 and 41 only clarify that a pardon of the principal penalty does not remit the accessory penalties unless the President says so; here the second sentence, “restored to his civil and political rights,” did. The right to seek elective office is a political right (RA 9225; ICCPR Art. 25(b)). The Monsanto concurrences requiring specific words are not controlling. (3) OEC Sec. 12’s plenary-pardon exception lifts the LGC Sec. 40(a) disqualification. (4) The third whereas clause is a statement of fact, not a condition: a preamble is not operative, the pardon states no condition or consequence of breach, and Arroyo stayed silent when he ran in 2010. (5) No whimsical or arbitrary act was shown.

iss.q: Did the COMELEC err in dismissing the petition because it had already resolved the pardon’s effect in 2010?
iss.why: The Court reduced all five issues to one question, the effect of the pardon, and decided it on the merits. Brion, J. (res judicata applies) and Leonen, J. (it does not) took opposite views.

iss.q: Should the second placer, Lim, be proclaimed Mayor?
iss.why: Estrada was qualified, so the intervention, which raised the same arguments, was dismissed with the petition.

risosvidal.vote: 11–3, Leonardo-de Castro, J. Mendoza, J., concurring; Brion, J. (on leave, left his vote), concurring. Leonen, J., dissenting, joined by Sereno, C.J., and Carpio, J. Jardeleza, J., took no part.
risosvidal.ops: Brion, J.: Lim cannot intervene for the first time in the Court; the pardon’s dispositive part prevails like a fallo; the Board of Pardons’ own definition of an absolute pardon is “restores … civil and political rights”; doubts are resolved for the grantee and the popular will; res judicata applies. Mendoza, J.: a condition must appear on the face of the pardon; the pardon restores rights, not innocence, and Manila’s voters judge his fitness. Leonen, J. (with Sereno, C.J., and Carpio, J.): Arts. 36 and 41 are requirements of form that do not reduce the power; “civil and political rights” is a basket, while the RPC singles out office and suffrage, which were never named; the whereas clause shows the premise of the pardon; Lim should be proclaimed. “By reading an ambiguity in favor of a convicted public officer, impunity is tolerated.”

iss.q: Should the petition be dismissed for forum shopping, defective notarization, or direct resort to the Court?
iss.why: The trial courts were asked for arrest warrants and hold-departure orders, the Court to strike down the proclamation: different issues and reliefs. Notarial defects are minor. Direct resort was justified because the questions (the limits of the power to revoke amnesty and the Bill of Rights) are purely legal and of first impression (GIOS-Samar).

iss.q: Is the validity of Proclamation No. 572 a political question?
iss.why: Under expanded judicial review, courts examine whether a branch stayed within constitutional limits, and the Bill of Rights is such a limit (Francisco; Diocese of Bacolod). Whether an amnesty was validly granted or is void is a justiciable question.

iss.q: Did Proclamation No. 75 unduly delegate the power to grant amnesty to the DND committee?
iss.why: The proclamation itself granted the amnesty to a class; the committee and the Secretary only checked membership in the class and compliance with the requirements, with no discretion. The Secretary acts as the President’s alter ego (qualified political agency), and the President cannot personally process 277 applications.

iss.q: May the President revoke a grant of amnesty without the concurrence of Congress?
iss.why: Sec. 19 is silent on revocation, but amnesty has always needed both the President’s grant and the legislature’s concurrence (1935, 1973, 1987): it exempts groups from the criminal law for a political end, and concurrence checks one person’s motives. Allowing unilateral revocation would make the concurrence futile and hold revocation like “a sword of Damocles” over grantees.

iss.q: Is Proclamation No. 572 unconstitutional?
iss.why: No warrantless arrest was ordered (“all lawful means” means a court warrant), and it is not a bill of attainder (it only removed a hurdle to trial). But it is an ex post facto measure: it strips a vested protection against prosecution, and the clause binds the Executive too. It violates double jeopardy: a dismissal on the ground of amnesty bars a new prosecution even though the accused moved for it, because amnesty obliterates the offense (Barrioquinto; RPC Art. 89). It violates due process: the DND decision had become final and immutable, and he was given no notice. And it violates equal protection: all 277 grantees’ forms were missing, but only his amnesty was voided (Biraogo).

iss.q: Did the coup d’état court rightly deny the motion for his arrest, finding that he applied and admitted guilt?
iss.why: The factual findings, affirmed by the CA, bind the Court. Failure to locate a form is not proof that none was filed; the certificate of amnesty issued only after review. On admission (Vera), it is enough to admit the covered acts and that they were criminal; his form acknowledged that his involvement violated the Constitution, criminal laws and the Articles of War. The dismissal order had long become final.

iss.q: Did the rebellion court gravely abuse its discretion in reviving the case and issuing a warrant?
iss.why: It declared its own final dismissal void on a mere motion and after only a summary hearing, denying due process; a final order can be attacked only by a separate action, and res judicata applied.

trillanesmedialdea.vote: 15–0, Singh, J. Leonen and Caguioa, JJ., concurring.
trillanesmedialdea.ops: Leonen, J.: would also void the proclamation as a bill of attainder and for the warrantless-arrest clause. Caguioa, J.: stresses that amnesty is a power shared by two branches, so revocation needs the same consensus as the grant, and that a presidential proclamation cannot do what an ex post facto law cannot.

iss.q: Is prohibition the proper remedy, and do the petitioners have standing?
iss.why: Given the public interest and the need for stability in the public service, early in the life of the 1987 Constitution, the Court set these procedural questions aside and decided the case, and let the CA intervene.

iss.q: Does the appointment of the Commissioner of Customs need confirmation by the Commission on Appointments?
iss.why: Only the first sentence of Sec. 16 speaks of nomination and CA consent; the second speaks only of appointment, and the records show why. The 1935 Constitution required confirmation of nearly everyone, which bred horse-trading; the 1973 Constitution required none. The framers chose a middle ground: they deleted “and bureaus” (Foz: bureau directors are “quite low” and confirmation would expose them to political influence) and made the second-sentence officers appointable without confirmation. “Also” means “in addition,” and limits on the appointing power are construed strictly. “Alone” is a carry-over from 1935 and redundant. The Customs Commissioner is a bureau head whom the law authorizes the President to appoint.

mison.vote: 9–2, Padilla, J. Cruz, J., dissented, joined by Gutierrez, Jr., J.
mison.ops: Cruz, J.: the second sentence continues the first and also requires confirmation; otherwise absurdities follow (a consul needs confirmation but the Central Bank Governor does not), “like checking the bridesmaids but forgetting the bride”; confirmation is the rule restored to check an appointing power Marcos abused. Gutierrez, Jr., J.: read all the appointment provisions together; only where the Constitution expressly dispenses with confirmation (judges, the Ombudsman, the VP in the Cabinet, lower officers by law) is it not required.

iss.q: May Congress, by law, require CA confirmation of presidential appointees beyond those in the first sentence of Sec. 16?
iss.why: The NLRC Chairman and Commissioners fall in the third group, officers the President is authorized by law to appoint. Requiring their confirmation (1) amends the first sentence by adding appointments that need consent and (2) amends the second by imposing consent on appointments entrusted to the President alone. The Court’s interpretation in Mison and Bautista is part of the law (Civil Code Art. 8), and the legislature cannot bind courts with its own reading (Endencia v. David). The framers deliberately left the 1935 system; the remedy is constitutional, not legislative.

calderon.vote: 12–1, Padilla, J. Cruz, J., dissenting; Bellosillo, J., took no part.
calderon.ops: Cruz, J., dissenting, on the strength of his Mison dissent: the Court should re-examine Mison instead of persisting in error out of adherence to precedent.

iss.q: Do the promotions of PNP officers to Chief Superintendent and Director need CA confirmation under Sec. 16 and RA 6975?
iss.why: The issue is not new: Mison, Bautista, Quintos-Deles and Calderon hold that only the first group needs confirmation, and Tarrosa v. Singson that Congress cannot expand the CA’s power. So Secs. 26 and 31 of RA 6975 are unconstitutional insofar as they require confirmation; being severable, the rest of the law stands. The presumption of constitutionality does not stop the Court from striking down a statute that transgresses the Constitution.

iss.q: Is the PNP akin to the AFP, so that police officers of a rank equal to colonel need confirmation?
iss.why: The Constitution distinguishes the armed forces (Art. XVI, Sec. 4) from “one police force, which shall be national in scope and civilian in character” (Sec. 6); RA 6975 itself says no element of the police shall be military. Police ranks are not military ranks.

iss.q: Did the Budget Secretary gravely abuse his discretion in paying the officers?
iss.why: The appointments were valid, so the disbursements were too.

manalo.vote: 13–0, Purisima, J. Puno, J., took no part. No separate opinions.

iss.q: Does the petitioner have standing?
iss.why: A citizen raising a constitutional question must show actual or threatened injury, fairly traceable to the act and redressable by a favorable ruling (TELEBAP; Bayan v. Zamora). Soriano showed none, and his suit was not a taxpayer’s suit because it did not involve Congress’s taxing power.

iss.q: Assuming standing, do the promotions of Coast Guard officers from naval captain up need CA confirmation?
iss.why: The clause on “officers of the armed forces from the rank of colonel or naval captain” refers to military officers alone, and the enumeration is exclusive (Mison; Calderon; Manalo). The Coast Guard is now under the DOTC and no longer part of the Navy or the AFP.

soriano.vote: 5–0, Corona, J. (Third Division). No separate opinions.

iss.q: Did the later ad interim appointments make the petition moot?
iss.why: The question whether acting secretaries may be appointed while Congress is in session will arise with every such appointment: capable of repetition yet evading review.

iss.q: Do the senators have standing?
iss.why: The CA is a constitutional body independent of Congress that exercises executive, not legislative, power when it consents (Cunanan v. Tan). So the acting appointments impaired no power of Congress; only the senators who sat on the CA (Enrile, Lacson, Angara, Ejercito-Estrada, Osmeña) had standing to protect its prerogatives.

iss.q: May the President appoint acting secretaries without CA consent while Congress is in session?
iss.why: The appointing power is executive, and Congress may only prescribe qualifications; it cannot name the appointee or force the President to make the undersecretary the acting secretary. An acting appointment is a temporary stop-gap, and a secretary is the President’s alter ego, so the temporary one must enjoy the President’s confidence. The Administrative Code (Book III, Sec. 17) allows designating “any other competent person” for at most one year; “law” includes the Constitution. The one-year limit guards against using acting appointments to circumvent confirmation, and here ad interim appointments followed at once.

iss.q: Should the Court resolve whether the respondents’ appointments violated the ban on midnight appointments?
iss.why: The Court will not pass on a constitutional question if the case can be disposed of on another ground. The decisive question was whether General had a cause of action for quo warranto against Urro.

iss.q: Was General’s appointment acting, and does the law bar acting appointments to the NAPOLCOM?
iss.why: The power to appoint includes temporary appointments unless specifically prohibited or the office is repugnant to it (Nacionalista Party v. Bautista: COMELEC). Staggered terms aim at continuity, not at barring acting appointments (Binamira v. Garrucho), and RA 8551 dropped them anyway; “unexpired term only” only prevents serving beyond the predecessor’s term. An acting appointee serves at pleasure, for at most one year; General’s appointment expired on July 21, 2009, and having served without protest, he was estopped from calling it permanent.

iss.q: Does General have a cause of action for quo warranto against Urro?
iss.why: A private quo warranto petitioner must show a clear right to the office (Rule 66, Secs. 5–6; Acosta v. Flor). An expired acting appointment, temporary and revocable at any time, gives none; the respondents’ titles can be tested in a proper case.

iss.q: Are the outgoing mayor’s appointments void “midnight appointments” under Art. VII, Sec. 15?
iss.why: Sec. 15 prohibits appointments by the President or Acting President two months before the next presidential election; “there is no law that prohibits local elective officials from making appointments during the last days of his or her tenure.” De Rama’s only reason was his belief that they were midnight appointments.

iss.q: May the petitioner rely on alleged fraud and irregularities raised only in a supplemental pleading and on appeal?
iss.why: They were contemporaneous with the appointments and should have been raised before the CSC; a supplemental pleading covers later events and its admission is discretionary; issues cannot be raised for the first time on appeal.

iss.q: Could the new mayor unilaterally recall the appointments?
iss.why: The appointees were screened by the selection board, qualified, attested by the CSC, and had assumed office, so they acquired a legal right that cannot be taken away except for cause, with notice and hearing (Aquino v. CSC; Mauna v. CSC). An accepted appointment cannot be withdrawn by the appointing authority; only the CSC may recall it, on grounds in its rules, and none was seasonably shown.

derama.vote: 9–6, Ynares-Santiago, J. Bellosillo, Puno and Vitug, JJ., concurred with notes. Mendoza, J., dissented, joined by Davide, C.J., Melo, Panganiban, Gonzaga-Reyes and De Leon, JJ.
derama.ops: Mendoza, J. (with five others): Sec. 15 applies a broader principle: an official who has lost an election is a caretaker who should not fill posts without urgent need; public office is a public trust, and Aytona v. Castillo struck down 350 last-hour appointments without any specific provision. The 14 appointments, made in 27 days after the loss, with perfunctory screening, were void.

iss.q: Do the petitioners have standing, and is there an actual, ripe controversy?
iss.why: Standing is waived for issues of transcendental importance, affecting the appointment of the Chief Justice and of judges amid many vacancies. The controversy is ripe: the JBC had begun the process and was undecided on whom to submit to; a reasonable certainty of the threatened constitutional injury suffices.

iss.q: Does the Sec. 15 election ban apply to appointments to the Supreme Court and the rest of the Judiciary?
iss.why: (1) The framers arranged the appointment rules by department; had they meant Sec. 15 to reach the Court, they would have said so in Art. VIII, Sec. 4(1), whose 90-day period is an imperative mandate to the President. (2) Sec. 15 targets Aytona-type midnight appointments and vote-buying; the JBC’s unhurried screening eliminates those evils. (3) Justice Regalado, a framer, confirmed the ban was not meant for the Court of Appeals. (4) Secs. 14 and 16 concern only executive appointments, so Sec. 15 between them does too. (5) Judicial independence. (6) The ban lasts 109 to 115 days, longer than 90, so applying it would make compliance impossible.

iss.q: Does the law on an Acting Chief Justice (Judiciary Act of 1948, Sec. 12) remove the need to appoint?
iss.why: The Chief Justice is appointed as such, never in an acting capacity; the Chief Justice heads the Judiciary and chairs the PET, and Chief Justices have historically been appointed the same or the next day.

iss.q: Does mandamus lie to compel the JBC to submit its list to the incumbent President?
iss.why: The JBC must submit its list before the vacancy so as not to shorten the President’s 90 days; that duty is ministerial, but it still had until May 17, 2010, and its choice of nominees is discretionary.

iss.q: Does prohibition lie against the JBC (because the Court appoints the Chief Justice, or because of the JBC’s composition)?
iss.why: Only the President appoints the Chief Justice, a “Member” of the Court. The challenge to the JBC’s composition was made by petitioners who were not nominees and so lacked standing on it.

decastrojbc.vote: Bersamin, J., with Leonardo-de Castro, Perez, Villarama and Abad, JJ.; Brion, J. (with Peralta, Del Castillo and Mendoza, JJ., in the result) concurring and dissenting; Nachura, J. (joined by Velasco, J.), separate opinion; Carpio Morales, J., dissenting. Puno, C.J., Carpio and Corona, JJ., took no part.
decastrojbc.ops: Carpio Morales, J., dissenting: the arrangement of articles is the weakest aid; the ban makes no distinction and its sole exception is exclusive; the framers kept it knowing of the JBC (Davide: a President could perpetuate himself through appointments to the Judiciary); the 90 days are suspended during the ban; the Court can work without an appointed Chief Justice. Brion, J.: the President may appoint the Chief Justice and Justices during the ban, a narrow exception, but Valenzuela should stand for lower-court judges given the hundreds of vacancies and local influence.

iss.q: Should the petition of Villanueva and Rosquita be dismissed outright?
iss.why: They filed a Rule 65 petition when a Rule 45 appeal was available, filed it late even as an appeal, and gave no reason for not seeking reconsideration.

iss.q: Are the petitioners’ appointments midnight appointments that violate Art. VII, Sec. 15?
iss.why: Both the ponencia and the dissent agreed that none showed the papers were issued and released before the ban. The dates the Records Office received them, the only reliable evidence of transmittal, fell within the ban, and all took their oaths during it.

iss.q: Is EO 2, which treats appointments accepted on or after March 11, 2010 and appointments to offices vacant only after that date as midnight appointments, constitutional?
iss.why: Appointment is a process ending in acceptance (Lacson v. Romero; Javier v. Reyes). Sec. 15 gave Aytona’s “stratagem to beat the deadline” a fixed, objective period, so appointments within it are automatically prohibited whatever the motive. Dropping acceptance would produce absurdities (an office deemed filled by someone who refuses it; incumbents removed by being appointed elsewhere) and invite antedating: it is easy to antedate papers, hard to simulate the whole process. Release through the Records Office proves transmittal; an office vacant only after the ban cannot be filled before it.

garafil.vote: 8–6, Carpio, J., with Sereno, C.J., Velasco, Del Castillo, Villarama, Reyes, Perlas-Bernabe and Leonen (on leave, left his vote), JJ. Brion, J., concurring and dissenting, joined by Leonardo-de Castro, Bersamin, Mendoza, Peralta and Perez, JJ. Jardeleza, J., took no part.
garafil.ops: Brion, J. (with five others): the President may interpret the Constitution, subject to review; by fixing a period, Sec. 15 removed any inquiry into bad faith, so the CA erred in deferring to the OP. But Sec. 15 uses “appointment” in the narrow sense, the President’s act of issuance; acceptance may follow, and the clause in EO 2 covering appointments dated before the ban but accepted during it is unconstitutional. Failure to course papers through the Records Office is not fatal. Still, none of these petitioners proved issuance before the ban, so their appointments fail.

iss.q: Does the petition satisfy the requisites of judicial review?
iss.why: Matibag’s reassignment rested on Benipayo’s authority as Chairman, so she had a personal stake in his title, and that constitutional question was the lis mota. The earliest opportunity means the first pleading before a competent court, not the date of filing. The issue was also of paramount public importance for the 2001 elections.

iss.q: Are ad interim appointments to the COMELEC the temporary or acting appointments that Art. IX-C, Sec. 1(2) prohibits?
iss.why: An ad interim appointment is permanent: it takes effect at once and cannot be withdrawn after the appointee qualifies; it ends only on disapproval or adjournment, resolutory conditions the Constitution itself sets. “Ad interim” describes the manner (made during recess), not the nature (PLM v. IAC). What Art. IX-C bars is the acting designation revocable at will (Brillantes v. Yorac; Nacionalista Party v. Bautista). Requiring confirmation before assumption would nullify the ad interim power, which here kept the COMELEC working through the 2001 elections; a confirmed majority remained.

iss.q: Does renewing by-passed ad interim appointments violate the ban on reappointment?
iss.why: A disapproval is final and cannot be renewed; a by-pass is no decision, so the President may renew (CA Rules, Sec. 17; Guevara v. Inocentes: the CA acts “only by action, never by omission”). The ban covers anyone confirmed for any term, but a lapsed ad interim appointment is not a term; “a reappointment presupposes a previous confirmed appointment.” The renewals kept the same term ending February 2, 2008, so no one serves beyond seven years.

iss.q: Was Matibag’s reassignment by the Chairman illegal?
iss.why: Benipayo was the de jure Chairman, and the Administrative Code lets the Chairman assign and transfer personnel. Matibag held only an acting appointment, lacking CES eligibility, so she had no security of tenure (Cuevas v. Bacal). COMELEC Resolution No. 3300 was the prior approval for election-period transfers; its notice requirement covers only field personnel.

iss.q: Did the finance officer exceed his authority in paying the appointees’ salaries?
iss.why: The appointments were valid, so the payments were too.

matibag.vote: 11–0, Carpio, J. Puno and Vitug, JJ., on official leave. No separate opinions.

iss.q: Does the President have power to discipline and remove a presidential appointee in the Career Executive Service?
iss.why: The power to remove is inherent in the power to appoint (Art. VII, Sec. 16), so Larin, appointed by the President, was under the President’s disciplining authority. But the power is not absolute: a career service officer has security of tenure and may be removed only for a cause provided by law and with due process.

iss.q: Was the investigation consistent with due process?
iss.why: Due process in administrative cases is a reasonable opportunity to be heard. Larin was asked to explain and submitted a position paper with supporting documents.

iss.q: Was Larin dismissed for a valid cause, given his acquittal?
iss.why: Administrative and criminal cases are generally independent. But the administrative charge rested entirely on the conviction, and the Court acquitted him on a categorical finding that the same acts were lawful and regular; with that basis gone, the administrative case must fall.

iss.q: May the President reorganize the BIR by executive order?
iss.why: The GAA (RA 7645, Sec. 62) allows organizational changes “directed by the President”; the Administrative Code’s residual powers carry PD 1416 as amended by PD 1772, still operative; the Constitution itself contemplates reorganizations. EO 127 (1987) was stale. The claim that the GAA provisions are riders fails against the presumption of constitutionality.

iss.q: Was the BIR reorganization tainted with bad faith?
iss.why: A reorganization is valid only in good faith (Dario v. Mison). EO 132 abolished offices and created another to absorb the same functions, and multiplied positions: badges of bad faith under RA 6656, Sec. 2. And permanent officers like Larin must be preferred for comparable new positions before outsiders are taken in (Sec. 4).

larin.vote: 13–0, Torres, Jr., J. Regalado, J., on leave. No separate opinions.

iss.q: Should the Court resolve the petition although Villar had stepped down?
iss.why: It was moot, but all four exceptions applied (David v. Macapagal-Arroyo): a grave constitutional issue, paramount public interest, the need for controlling principles, and capability of repetition.

iss.q: Does Funa, as taxpayer and citizen, have standing?
iss.why: The case is of transcendental importance, so the Court relaxed the direct-injury requirement.

iss.q: Is certiorari a proper remedy, rather than declaratory relief or quo warranto?
iss.why: Certiorari lies to inquire whether an appointment infringed the Constitution or was made with grave abuse of discretion.

iss.q: Is Villar’s appointment as COA Chairman, after four years as Commissioner, valid?
iss.why: (1) A promotion is not a barred reappointment, which means a second appointment to the same office; the framers (Aquino, Monsod, Foz) contemplated “upgrading” within a seven-year total; Matibag’s fourth situation was obiter and is abandoned. (2) But no one may serve more than seven years in all, so a fresh term to 2015 was impossible. (3) Carague’s seat fell vacant by expiration, which requires a full seven-year appointment; the President cannot split terms by giving a shorter one. So Villar could not be validly appointed under any term.

funavillar.vote: 12–3 on unconstitutionality, Velasco, J. Carpio, J. (with Abad and Sereno, JJ.) concurring and dissenting; Mendoza, J. (with Brion and Reyes, JJ.) concurring and dissenting, would uphold the appointment.
funavillar.ops: Carpio, J.: the Constitution bans reappointment of any kind, promotions included; both the acting and permanent chairmanships were void. Mendoza, J.: a promotion is allowed even to a seat vacated by expiration, as long as the total service stays within seven years (as with COMELEC’s Garcia in 1959); Villar could serve until his Commissioner term ended.

iss.q: Are the requisites of judicial review, including standing, present?
iss.why: They were not in issue; Funa sued as taxpayer, citizen and lawyer on a question of constitutional importance.

iss.q: Did the appointment of a new Solicitor General make the case moot?
iss.why: The case falls under the exceptions: a grave constitutional question, capable of repetition, needing a controlling rule.

iss.q: Did Agra’s concurrent designations violate Art. VII, Sec. 13?
iss.why: As Acting Secretary of Justice he was covered by Sec. 13, whose only exceptions are the Constitution’s own and ex officio posts (Civil Liberties Union). The acting nature of a designation does not matter: “to hold an office” is to occupy and discharge it, and a contrary reading would open the floodgates to circumvention (Funa v. Ermita). The Solicitor General’s functions are neither derived from nor required by the DOJ’s; the OSG is independent and autonomous. And even if the Acting Solicitor General were outside Sec. 13, the two offices are incompatible under Art. IX-B, Sec. 7(2).

iss.q: Do Agra’s official acts as Acting Secretary of Justice remain valid?
iss.why: He was not a de jure officer, but he held the office under color of a known appointment, so he was a de facto officer whose acts bind the public and third persons.

iss.q: Does Funa have standing?
iss.why: As in his earlier public-law cases, the Court recognized his standing as taxpayer, citizen and lawyer.

iss.q: Did RA 10149 make the case moot?
iss.why: The designation could have ended or become invalid under the new law, but the case falls under the exceptions to mootness.

iss.q: Is the CSC Chairman’s ex officio designation to the four boards valid?
iss.why: Commissioners fall under the general rule (Art. IX-B, Sec. 7(2)), read with Art. IX-A, Sec. 2, which bars them from other office during tenure. (1) The Administrative Code provision is valid: matters affecting government employees’ careers and welfare are primary CSC functions. (2) But these boards also exercise corporate powers unrelated to personnel, and the designation carried per diems, so it was not a true ex officio post. (3) The CSC Chairman cannot sit on bodies under the President’s control without impairing the commission’s independence (Art. IX-A, Sec. 1).

iss.q: Do Duque’s acts as a board member remain valid?
iss.why: He was not a de jure officer but a de facto officer during his tenure.

funacsc.vote: 13–0, Bersamin, J. Brion, J., on leave; Perlas-Bernabe, J., on official leave. No separate opinions.

iss.q: Did Gaminde’s term as CSC Commissioner expire on February 2, 1999, as her appointment stated?
iss.why: The rotational plan needs the first terms to start on a common date and vacancies to be filled only for the unexpired balance (Republic v. Imperial); under the 1987 Constitution that date is February 2, 1987. The transitory provision (Art. XVIII, Sec. 15) governs the tenure of incumbents, not the terms in Art. IX. So the five-year seat’s first term ran to 1992 and the second to February 2, 1999; she was bound by the term in the appointment she accepted, and the legal counsel’s contrary letter was wrong.

iss.q: Did the COA err in disallowing her and her staff’s salaries from February 2, 1999 to February 2, 2000?
iss.why: She stayed on in good faith as a de facto officer and actually served, so she and her co-terminous staff are entitled to pay for that period.

gaminde.vote: Pardo, J. Eleven Justices on the term (Puno, J., in the result); De Leon, J., concurring and dissenting, joined by Mendoza, J. Bellosillo, J., took no part. All agreed the pay should not be disallowed.
gaminde.ops: De Leon, J. (with Mendoza, J.): the first appointees’ terms began on February 2, 1988, so Gaminde’s term ended on February 2, 2000; he agreed the pay could not be disallowed.

iss.q: Is RA 6770, Sec. 8(3), giving a successor Ombudsman a full term, unconstitutional?
iss.why: The law is presumed valid and the petitioner did not show a clear breach. The Office of the Ombudsman is not a collegial constitutional commission; Art. XI, Sec. 10 equates the Ombudsman and Deputies with the commissions only in rank and salary. The 7-5-3 rotational plan is unique to the commissions, so Gaminde does not apply. The Constitution nowhere limits a successor to the unexpired term, so every appointee, for an expired or unexpired term, serves a full seven years from appointment.

iss.q: Is certiorari the proper remedy, rather than quo warranto?
iss.why: The petition primarily attacks the constitutionality of a law; the officers’ de facto status was sought only as a consequence, so it is not a collateral attack on title (unlike Topacio v. Ong).

iss.q: May the petitioner come directly to the Supreme Court?
iss.why: Under its expanded power of review, given the constitutional question raised, the Court took cognizance despite the hierarchy of courts.

ifurung.vote: 14–0, Martires, J. Sereno, C.J., on leave. No separate opinions.

iss.q: (2012) Does the Office of the President have disciplinary power over a Deputy Ombudsman and the Special Prosecutor under RA 6770, Sec. 8(2)?
iss.why: Officers the President appoints are generally removable by him, unless the Constitution vests removal elsewhere; the President appoints the Deputies (Art. XI, Sec. 9), so Sec. 8(2) only made express an implied power, shared concurrently with the Ombudsman, limited to the impeachment grounds and subject to due process. The constitutional challenge failed because the Court was equally divided.

iss.q: (2012) Was Gonzales denied due process when the OP decided without his attendance?
iss.why: He was given notice and the chance to answer; he chose not to attend the clarificatory conference.

iss.q: (2012) Did the OP gravely abuse its discretion in dismissing Gonzales for betrayal of public trust?
iss.why: Betrayal of public trust must involve bad faith and gravity comparable to the other impeachment grounds. Gonzales acted on the draft within nine days; the delay lay largely in the Ombudsman’s office. He was reinstated with backwages, without prejudice to the Ombudsman’s investigation.

iss.q: (2012) Are the proceedings against the Special Prosecutor premature while the plea bargain is pending in the Sandiganbayan?
iss.why: The administrative case concerns her conduct, independent of the criminal case’s outcome.

iss.q: (2014) Is Sec. 8(2) unconstitutional insofar as it lets the President discipline and remove a Deputy Ombudsman?
iss.why: The question is justiciable. The Ombudsman’s independence is similar in degree and kind to the constitutional commissions’ (Brillantes v. Yorac; Macalintal), and the framers made it independent of the Executive precisely because many culprits are in the executive branch. Letting the President discipline Deputies, while the President’s own officials are subject to the Ombudsman, endangers that independence. Congress’s power to provide for the removal of non-impeachable officers is not carte blanche.

iss.q: (2014) Is Sec. 8(2) unconstitutional as to the Special Prosecutor?
iss.why: By a separate vote, the Office of the Special Prosecutor is not constitutionally within the Office of the Ombudsman and does not share its independence (the prevailing view in Leonen, J.’s opinion).

iss.q: (2014) Even assuming OP authority, was Gonzales’s dismissal correct?
iss.why: Alternatively, the OP’s finding of betrayal of public trust was patently erroneous; but the ruling on Sec. 8(2) made further ruling on the dismissal unnecessary.

gonzalesiii.vote: 2012: Perlas-Bernabe, J.; Carpio, J., concurring; Brion, J. (with Velasco, Leonardo-de Castro and Perez, JJ.) and Abad, J. (joined by Bersamin, J.) dissenting. 2014: Brion, J., 8–7 on the Deputies; Perlas-Bernabe, J. (with Sereno, C.J., Carpio, Peralta, Del Castillo, Villarama and Reyes, JJ.) and Leonen, J., concurring and dissenting.
gonzalesiii.ops: 2012: Carpio, J.: independence does not mean exclusive disciplinary authority; Sec. 8(2) is valid. Brion, J., and Abad, J.: Sec. 8(2) is unconstitutional; the OP proceedings should be voided. 2014: Perlas-Bernabe, J.: would uphold Sec. 8(2) entirely. Leonen, J.: Sec. 8(2) fails as to the Deputies but stands as to the Special Prosecutor, and there was substantial evidence against Gonzales, whom the Ombudsman may still discipline.

iss.q: Did Proclamation No. 1946 and AOs 273 and 273-A violate local autonomy (Art. X, Sec. 16; RA 9054)?
iss.why: The DILG Secretary never took over the ARMM. When the Governor was taken into custody, succession under RA 9054 ran its course: the Vice-Governor became Governor and the Speaker acting Vice-Governor. The region stayed in the hands of its own officials, so the Court did not need to rule on “transfer” versus “delegation” of supervision.

iss.q: Did the President invalidly exercise emergency powers when she called out the AFP and PNP in Maguindanao, Sultan Kudarat and Cotabato City?
iss.why: Emergency powers under Art. VI, Sec. 23(2) need war or other national emergency and a law by which Congress authorizes the President, for a limited period and with restrictions. She declared only a state of emergency in three places, not a national emergency, and acted under no such law. Calling out the armed forces is a power the Constitution vests directly in the President, needing no congressional authority.

iss.q: Did the President have factual bases for declaring the state of emergency and calling out the armed forces?
iss.why: The Commander-in-Chief may call out the armed forces “whenever it becomes necessary” (Sanlakas). The Court may inquire into the factual basis (Lacson v. Perez) but defers unless grave abuse is shown, and the petitioner must prove the absence of basis (IBP v. Zamora). The petitioners showed only that some areas had no violent incidents. The OSG showed the clans’ armed followers (about 2,400 men on one side, 1,800 on the other), reports of planned retaliation and armed men moving: preventive action was justified.

ampatuan.ops: None; the Justices concurred in the ponencia.

iss.q: Did the lifting of martial law and the restoration of the writ by Proclamation No. 1963 render the petitions moot?
iss.why: The Court decides a constitutional question only if it is unavoidable (Biraogo). The President withdrew the proclamation before Congress could act, a supervening event that ended the controversy, and it was never meaningfully implemented: no military takeover of local governments, no decrees, no mass arrests; those arrested were released or charged. Unlike Lansang and Aquino v. Enrile, the Court never examined the President’s evidence; and the trial court’s ruling in the rebellion case could not substitute for the Court’s review.

iss.q: Is the power to proclaim martial law or suspend the writ exercised jointly and sequentially by the President and Congress, so that with no congressional action and the proclamation lifted, the Court has nothing to review?
iss.why: The President and Congress “act in tandem”: the President initiates, but only Congress can maintain the proclamation. Since congressional review is automatic, the Court must let Congress act first; the matter is “first a political question in the hands of Congress before it becomes a justiciable one in the hands of the Court,” which steps in as the “final rampart” only if Congress defaults. (Lagman v. Medialdea, 2017, later set this aside.)

iss.q: Does the case fall under the exceptions to the moot-and-academic rule?
iss.why: The proclamation looked “more like saber-rattling” than an actual deployment and arbitrary use of political power, unlike the martial law of the late 1960s and 1970s. The Court will not decide purely academic questions for scholarly interest, and avoids constitutional questions unless “avoidance becomes evasion.”

iss.q: Did Proclamation No. 1959 have sufficient factual basis (actual rebellion, with public safety requiring it), and the related questions: standing, the meaning of “rebellion,” warrantless arrests, conflicting reviews by the Court and Congress?
iss.why: Having found the case moot, the Court did not reach them. Carpio, J., dissenting, would have held that any citizen has standing, that “rebellion” means Art. 134 of the RPC, that martial law authorizes no warrantless arrests beyond Rule 113, that the Court’s ruling on factual basis is not needed to judge related acts, and that there was no actual rebellion in Maguindanao.

fortun.vote: 8–6. Abad, J., with Leonardo-de Castro, Brion, Peralta, Bersamin, Villarama, Jr. and Mendoza, JJ.; Perez, J., concurred in the dismissal in a separate opinion. Dissenting: Carpio, J. (joined by Sereno, Reyes and Perlas-Bernabe, JJ.) and Velasco, Jr., J. (joined by Corona, C.J.). Del Castillo, J., on leave.
fortun.ops: Carpio, J., dissenting: Sec. 18 gives “any citizen” standing; all four exceptions to mootness apply, and voluntary cessation does not oust jurisdiction, or a President could declare martial law without basis and lift it before review; rebellion means Art. 134 of the RPC, shown by probable cause; martial law does not suspend the Bill of Rights, and suspending the writ does not validate illegal arrests; Congress’s power is to revoke, “not to confirm or ratify,” so the Court may review even if Congress has not acted; and since the 1987 text deleted “imminent danger,” there was no actual rebellion. Velasco, Jr., J., also dissented.

iss.q: Do the petitioners have standing, including the representatives who sued as such?
iss.why: Sec. 18 allows “any citizen” to file; the representatives were treated as citizens.

iss.q: Are the petitions the “appropriate proceeding” under Sec. 18, par. 3?
iss.why: The proceeding is not certiorari, which tests grave abuse and would emasculate the review of sufficiency the framers wanted. Sec. 18 constitutionalizes Lansang (rejecting Garcia-Padilla) as a safeguard on top of Art. VIII, Sec. 1. It is unique: any citizen may file, the only question is the sufficiency of the factual basis, and the Court must decide within 30 days.

iss.q: Is the Court’s review independent of what Congress does?
iss.why: The Court’s review is passive (on a citizen’s petition) and looks at the facts at the time of the proclamation; Congress’s review is automatic and may consider later facts. The two do not depend on each other; Fortun’s contrary view is set aside.

iss.q: May the Court calibrate the President’s choice among calling out, suspending the writ and martial law; and is the Defense Secretary’s recommendation required?
iss.why: The graduation of powers refers to their scope and effect, not to a sequence the President must follow; the choice is the President’s. The framers dropped any requirement of prior concurrence, and no recommendation from the Defense Secretary is needed.

iss.q: Is Proclamation No. 216 void for vagueness, for including “other rebel groups” and lacking operational guidelines?
iss.why: The void-for-vagueness doctrine is a free-speech tool and the proclamation regulates conduct (David). “Other rebel groups” is explained by Proclamation No. 55, and guidelines are not part of the factual basis.

iss.q: Would voiding Proclamation No. 216 recall Proclamation No. 55 or the calling out of the armed forces?
iss.why: Calling out is a separate power (Kulayan v. Tan), and the operative fact doctrine would protect acts done in reliance on it.

iss.q: What must the Court look at: accuracy or sufficiency, which facts, what standard and whose burden?
iss.a: Sufficiency; facts at the time; probable cause
iss.why: The Court checks sufficiency, not accuracy; the Lansang arbitrariness test is done away with. It looks at the facts known to the President at the time (the Proclamation and the Report), in their totality; later events only guide, and falsus in uno does not apply. Actual rebellion and public safety must concur, and the President needs only probable cause (Carpio, J., in Fortun). Rebellion is defined by Art. 134 of the RPC: a public uprising and taking up arms, for the purpose of removing territory from allegiance or depriving the President or Congress of powers.

iss.q: Was there sufficient factual basis for martial law and the suspension of the writ: (a) actual rebellion; (b) public safety?
iss.why: The uprising was conceded; its purpose (a wilayat, ISIS flags) was to remove Marawi and Mindanao from allegiance and deprive the President of his powers. The petitioners’ counter-evidence was news reports, hearsay twice removed, and it attacked only five facts; the rest stood unrebutted. Public safety required it: civilians attacked, hostages taken, services cut, reinforcements blocked.

iss.q: Did the hostilities justify martial law over the whole of Mindanao?
iss.why: The Constitution lets the President cover “the Philippines or any part thereof,” and the Court lacks the military machinery to second-guess the area. Rebellion is not confined within predetermined bounds; Marawi was a staging point, and the Abu Sayyaf, Maute and BIFF were linked, with violence elsewhere (Basilan, Sulu, Bohol).

iss.q: Do terrorist acts negate rebellion, or equal it?
iss.why: Terrorism neither negates nor absorbs rebellion; what matters is the purpose. RA 9372 cannot curtail the President’s powers under the Constitution.

iss.q: (Resolution, December 5, 2017) Did the expiry of Proclamation No. 216 moot the challenge to its factual basis?
iss.why: A presidential proclamation lasts at most 60 days and terminates automatically (a “time fuse”). The extension, initiated by the President but approved by Congress, is a separate act, a joint act of the President and Congress; the petitions assailed only the proclamation. The Court nonetheless saw “no reason to disturb” its findings.

iss.q: (Resolution) Must the Court determine the accuracy, not just the sufficiency, of the factual basis?
iss.why: Accuracy is a higher standard. The Court reviews the totality of the facts known to the President before and at the declaration; later events are irrelevant, and some inaccurate facts do not invalidate it if the others show rebellion and public safety. Probable cause means rebellion is “more likely than not.”

iss.q: (Resolution) Did the Court abdicate its power of review by deferring to the Executive?
iss.why: Its findings came after weighing the Proclamation, the Report and a closed-door briefing by the Defense Secretary and the AFP Chief. Martial law needs actual rebellion, so time is of the essence, and it has no exact metes and bounds: it may spill over beyond the place of the uprising.
