lagman17.vote: 11–4. Del Castillo, J., with Velasco, Jr., Leonardo-de Castro, Peralta, Bersamin, Mendoza, Reyes, Perlas-Bernabe (in the result), Jardeleza, Martires and Tijam, JJ. Dissenting: Sereno, C.J. and Caguioa, J. (valid only in Lanao del Sur, Maguindanao and Sulu), Carpio, J. (valid only in Marawi City) and Leonen, J. (void entirely). The motions for reconsideration were denied on December 5, 2017, 10–4.
lagman17.ops: Carpio, J.: valid only in Marawi City; the Proclamation itself spoke of “this part of Mindanao,” and fear of spread is the “imminent danger” the framers deleted; the burden is on the Government. Sereno, C.J.: valid only in Lanao del Sur, Maguindanao and Sulu, the “nesting grounds” of the groups; necessity requires proportionality and defined bounds, or martial law reaches “places as terrorism and rebellion-free as Dinagat Islands or Camiguin.” Caguioa, J.: a “neutral and straightforward fact-checking mechanism”; public safety did not require martial law over all of Mindanao; on reconsideration, accuracy is inseparable from sufficiency. Leonen, J.: terrorism, not rebellion; an undefined declaration is void for vagueness; “The terrorist wins when we suspend all that we believe in.” Among the concurrences, Jardeleza, Mendoza and Perlas-Bernabe, JJ. preferred a reasonableness standard, and Leonardo-de Castro and Martires, JJ. would allow certiorari as a vehicle.

iss.q: Is the failure to attach a copy of RBH No. 4 fatal?
iss.why: The Court takes judicial notice of it, and the OSG annexed it.

iss.q: May the President be impleaded?
iss.why: The President is immune from suit during tenure (Rubrico; David) and was dropped as respondent.

iss.q: Is Congress an indispensable party?
iss.why: The extension is the act of the whole Congress, not just its leaders, so Congress must be joined (Rule 3, Sec. 7). One petition impleaded Congress, and the OSG answered for all.

iss.q: Are the petitioners barred by conclusiveness of judgment (Lagman v. Medialdea; Padilla) from questioning the persistence of the rebellion?
iss.why: The parties were the same but not the issue: the earlier case decided the existence of rebellion; this one, its persistence. A ruling on factual basis is “transitory” because facts change.

iss.q: May the Court review the extension under its expanded certiorari jurisdiction, and how far?
iss.a: NO; only the sufficiency of the factual basis
iss.why: Sec. 18, par. 3 is a special proceeding (Lagman v. Medialdea); review is limited to the sufficiency of the factual basis.

iss.q: Is the manner in which Congress deliberated (the joint session rules) subject to review?
iss.why: Each House determines its own rules (Art. VI, Sec. 16(3)); courts intervene only for a constitutional violation (Arroyo v. De Venecia), limited to quorum, voting and publication. The rules were adopted without objection.

iss.q: May Congress extend martial law more than once and for longer than 60 days?
iss.why: Sec. 18 is silent on the number; its only limits are the President’s initiative, the persistence of rebellion with public safety, and the Court’s review. It says “for a period to be determined by the Congress,” and “in the same manner” refers to voting jointly by a majority of all Members, not to the period. A proposal to cap extensions at 60 days was not adopted.

iss.q: Was there sufficient factual basis for the extension: does the rebellion persist (including other groups and the NPA), does public safety require it, and should proportionality tests apply?
iss.why: About 400 new recruits (roughly the Marawi force), 185 at large, 48 foreign fighters and a financial build-up showed the rebellion persisted; it is a continuing crime, not only a clash of arms, and the BIFF and NPA could be counted, Congress having made the collective judgment. Public safety: 2,781 rebels, 3,211 firearms, 537 affected barangays and bomb plots. The Court rejected a “cannot govern” test and proportionality or suitability tests as intrusions on the President’s prerogative; safeguards remain (early lifting, new petitions, separate cases for abuses).

iss.q: Are the petitioners entitled to a TRO or injunction?
iss.why: They showed no right in esse, and the alleged abuses were neither proved nor linked to the extension.

lagmanpimentel.vote: 10–5. Tijam, J. Dissenting: Sereno, C.J., Carpio, Leonen, Jardeleza and Caguioa, JJ.
lagmanpimentel.ops: Sereno, C.J.: martial law is the law of necessity; the Court must calibrate gravity, area and period, and recruitment and bomb plots show at most imminent danger; adding the NPA to show persistence is “self-contradictory.” Carpio, J.: “persist” means the same Maute rebellion, which ended with Marawi’s liberation; capability is not rebellion; an NPA rebellion needs its own 60-day proclamation first. Leonen, J.: Sec. 18 requires heightened scrutiny; an undefined request is a “carte blanche,” and three-minute interpellations stifled deliberation. Jardeleza, J.: public safety requires scale: sustained armed hostilities and groups holding territory. Caguioa, J.: the triggering rebellion must persist; new groups need a new declaration, or there will be an endless chain of extensions. Bersamin, J. (concurring): the Sec. 18 proceeding involves no rights of parties, so no one is indispensable.

iss.q: Was there sufficient factual basis for the third extension: does the rebellion persist, does public safety require it, and was the extension necessary?
iss.why: The standard is sufficiency, not grave abuse, and the Court need not make its own findings (Montenegro). Probable cause suffices, and the test is reasonableness, not accuracy; reports not palpably false are read in their totality, with Congress’s concurrence making them “weightier.” The Abu Sayyaf, BIFF, Dawlah Islamiyah and NPA continue the rebellion: a missing motive does not negate it, it is a continuing crime with no fixed time or place, and it includes propaganda and recruitment (Aquino v. Enrile). The peace and order councils’ resolutions showed public safety required it; necessity was absorbed in these findings.

iss.q: Does the Constitution limit the number or the length of extensions?
iss.why: Sec. 18 leaves the period “to be determined by the Congress”; the limits are only the President’s initiative, persistence with public safety, and review. The 60-day cap proposed in the Constitutional Commission was rejected.

iss.q: Did Proclamation No. 216 become functus officio when the Marawi siege ended?
iss.why: The end of the siege was not the end of the rebellion: remnants of the Hapilon-Maute group were recruiting and rebuilding, and kidnappings, arson, bombings and murders are absorbed in rebellion, a continuing crime (Lagman v. Pimentel).

iss.q: Is the manner in which Congress approved the extension reviewable?
iss.why: Each House determines its own rules, including time limits on interpellation; courts intervene only where the rules violate the Constitution or are arbitrary (quorum, voting, publication).

iss.q: May the extension be struck down for grave abuse of discretion by Congress?
iss.why: The Sec. 18 standard is the sufficiency of the factual basis, not grave abuse, so the question was not reached.

iss.q: Do alleged human rights violations in implementing martial law void its extension?
iss.why: They must be resolved in separate proceedings. Martial law does not suspend the Constitution; the Bill of Rights and the courts remain, with remedies under RA 7438, RA 9372, RA 9745, amparo and habeas data.

lagman19.vote: 9–4. Carandang, J., with Bersamin, C.J. and Del Castillo, J.; Peralta, Perlas-Bernabe (in the result), A. Reyes, Jr., Gesmundo, J. Reyes, Jr. and Hernando, JJ., concurring separately. Dissenting: Carpio, Leonen, Jardeleza and Caguioa, JJ.
lagman19.ops: Carpio, J.: an extension needs the same rebellion as the original proclamation, which ended with Hapilon’s death and Marawi’s liberation; the Government bears the burden. Leonen, J.: martial law is a last resort for a State that “drifts between life and death”; the reports were defective and the NPA an afterthought; an “enfeebled Supreme Court.” Jardeleza, J.: rebellion exists but lacks the scale public safety requires, and the Government’s own figures fell from 2017 to 2018. Caguioa, J.: of 150 incidents, 54 had no identified perpetrator and about 90% no motive; no one was charged with rebellion in 2018; at most a threat, and “imminent danger” was deleted. Peralta, J. (concurring): rebellion is “like cancer”; the 30-day period may not always be met.

iss.q: Should the petitions for habeas corpus be dismissed as moot?
iss.why: The only question in habeas corpus is the legality of the detention, and all the petitioners had been released.

iss.q: Do military commissions have jurisdiction to try civilians for offenses committed during martial law while the civil courts are open and functioning, and should Aquino, Jr. v. Military Commission No. 2 be abandoned?
iss.why: Due process requires trial by judicial process, not executive or military process. Military commissions are not courts in the judicial system, where judicial power is vested exclusively; they are instruments of the Commander-in-Chief to discipline the armed forces. As long as civil courts function, as they did during martial law, military trial of civilians denies due process, and the judgment is void. Precedent cannot prevail over constitutionalism: Aquino, Jr. and its progeny are abandoned. Art. VII, Sec. 18 of the 1987 Constitution confirms the rule.

iss.q: Even assuming it had jurisdiction, was MC 34 ousted of it for disregarding the petitioners’ rights?
iss.why: Deprivation of a constitutional right ousts a tribunal of jurisdiction (Gumabon). The record was incomplete, witnesses were not subpoenaed, the evidence was deemed waived, and death was imposed after a 25-minute recess.

iss.q: Did Proclamation No. 2045 divest MC 34 of authority over civilians, and does double jeopardy bar a trial in the civil courts?
iss.why: Aquino, Jr. rested on the emergency; with martial law lifted, the commissions became functus officio as to civilians, whose cases go to the civil courts. Double jeopardy needs a first tribunal of competent jurisdiction, which MC 34 was not.

olaguer.vote: 13–0. Gancayco, J.; Teehankee, C.J., concurring. Padilla, J., took no part.
olaguer.ops: Teehankee, C.J., concurring: the petitioners were also denied an impartial tribunal, since the alleged targets of the plot, the President and the Defense Minister, approved the charges, reviewed the judgment and controlled the commissioners’ careers; he recounts the five-year ordeal, hails the reinstated ouster-of-jurisdiction rule and lists the 1987 checks on martial law. “The greatest threat to freedom is the shortness of human memory.”

iss.q: May the writ of habeas corpus issue to release a person serving a final judgment of conviction, on the basis of post-conviction DNA evidence?
iss.why: Habeas corpus reaches illegal restraint, but not restraint under the lawful process of a competent court. After a final conviction it lies only for (a) a denied constitutional right resulting in the restraint, (b) lack of jurisdiction to impose the sentence, or (c) an excessive penalty (Feria v. CA). It is not a writ of error and does not re-weigh evidence. The petition alleged none of the grounds; counsel’s withdrawal mid-appeal was not a denial of the right to counsel; and what it really sought was a new appreciation of the evidence.

iss.q: May a new trial be granted on the DNA results as newly discovered evidence?
iss.why: A motion for new trial must be filed before the judgment becomes final (Rule 121), and the evidence could have been obtained with reasonable diligence. Paternity is not an element of rape (pregnancy is not), though it bears on the award of support; the conviction rested on the victim’s testimony.

devilla.vote: 14–0. Ynares-Santiago, J.; Carpio, J. and Callejo, Sr., J. concurring (Davide, C.J. and Panganiban, J. joining both). Corona, J., on leave.
devilla.ops: Carpio, J.: the door stays open for exonerating DNA evidence: under its power to protect constitutional rights (Art. VIII, Sec. 5(5)), the Court may order a new trial, without vacating the conviction, if DNA testing that was not available at trial would show the convict could not have committed the crime (for example, semen that does not match). Callejo, Sr., J.: such a remedy is sui generis until Rule 121 is revised.

iss.q: Do the petitioners have standing?
iss.why: Taxpayers may question government contracts entered into against the law (Tatad v. Garcia); the case concerns the deflection of public funds, sets a precedent for future debt contracts, and involves a debt of ₱3.80 trillion, almost half of it foreign: transcendental importance.

iss.q: Is the claim that the agreements waived the right to repudiate void or fraudulent (“behest”) loans ripe?
iss.why: No behest loans were shown to be covered; fraudulent loans are voidable and void ones must be declared so, so the right is contingent; unilateral repudiation would invite sanctions; and the agreements had a no-waiver clause anyway. The choice is the Executive’s.

iss.q: Are the buyback and bond-conversion schemes within the President’s power to “contract or guarantee foreign loans” (Art. VII, Sec. 20)?
iss.why: Both extinguish old debt. A bond buyer lends money to the issuer, so a bond is a loan; the provision makes no distinction among kinds of loans, and reading one in would be “the worst kind of judicial legislation.” RA 245 allows bonds for purchase, redemption and refunding. A buyback is an implied incident of borrowing (one who may borrow may pay, restructure or refuse), and automatic appropriations for debt service (PD 1177; Guingona v. Carague) and RA 240 let the Finance Secretary redeem debt before maturity.

iss.q: May the Secretary of Finance and the debt negotiators exercise the borrowing power as the President’s alter egos?
iss.why: Under qualified political agency, department heads are alter egos (Villena). Only powers that suspend freedoms or override other branches (martial law, the writ, pardon) must be exercised personally; borrowing is established governance. The President’s prior approval or later ratification is needed, but none was shown lacking, so it is presumed.

iss.q: Does the Financing Program violate state policies (Art. II, Secs. 9, 10, 19), amounting to grave abuse?
iss.why: Even on the petitioners’ figures the program brought debt relief. State policies are not a panacea, and whether there was a better way is a question of wisdom; judicial review checks, it does not supplant.

constantino.vote: Tinga, J., with eleven Justices concurring; Davide, C.J. and Puno, J. concurred in the result; Panganiban, J., filed a separate opinion. No dissent.

iss.q: Is President Duterte a proper respondent?
iss.why: He is immune from suit during his tenure (De Lima v. Duterte) and was dropped.

iss.q: Are the requisites of judicial review present: standing, an actual case, and the moot prayer for documents?
iss.a: YES, except as to the waiver-of-immunity clause
iss.why: The petitioners have standing given the transcendental importance of public contracts and foreign debt; the signing itself is a government act, and specific clauses are assailed. The prayer for documents is moot (they were released) but was addressed as capable of repetition yet evading review.

iss.q: Should the petitions be dismissed for violating the hierarchy of courts?
iss.why: Direct resort is allowed because the questions are purely legal (GIOS-Samar).

iss.q: Is prohibition unavailable because the loans were a fait accompli?
iss.why: A contract passes through negotiation, perfection and consummation; disbursements were conditional and nothing had been repaid. Negotiation is an executive prerogative, so it would be absurd to require suit any earlier.

iss.q: Are the loan agreements void for lacking the Monetary Board’s prior concurrence (Art. VII, Sec. 20)?
iss.why: The requirement, born of the Marcos-era debt, gives the central bank, as custodian of reserves, a say on paying capacity. It works through the procedure laid down by law and regulation: an Approval-in-Principle before negotiations, review of the documents, and Final Approval after signing but before drawdown. Only the first is strictly “prior,” but the Board’s role continues; Leonen, J.’s view that Final Approval must precede signing is too strict, and a looser rule would repeat history. Both loans followed the procedure.

iss.q: Does the confidentiality clause unduly restrict public access to information on foreign loans (Art. XII, Sec. 21)?
iss.why: Information on foreign loans “shall be made available to the public”: it cannot be kept secret wholesale, made subject to the lender’s consent, or limited to government use.

iss.q: Do the conditions for releasing funds (an advance to the Chinese contractor) violate the Filipino First policy and the procurement law?
iss.a: NO, as to the loan agreements
iss.why: The loans are not the award, which came through notes verbale and limited bidding; Filipino First is not a Filipino monopoly; the notes and loans are executive agreements that allow a different procurement procedure (RA 9184, Sec. 4). But limiting the bidding to three Chinese contractors apparently contravened Filipino First; the Court did not void it because it was not prayed for.

iss.q: Do the arbitration clauses (Chinese law; CIETAC or HKIAC) violate an independent foreign policy (Art. II, Sec. 7)?
iss.why: Parties may choose the governing law and forum (party autonomy); the harm is speculative, and foreign law must be proved.

iss.q: Does the waiver-of-immunity clause offend the provisions on national economy and patrimony?
iss.why: Not ripe: there has been no default, arbitration or seizure.

colmenares.vote: 13–1. J.Y. Lopez, J.; Caguioa, Lazaro-Javier and Gaerlan, JJ., concurring; Leonen, J., dissenting.
colmenares.ops: Leonen, J., dissenting: an Approval-in-Principle with bare data is not concurrence; without a contract the Board cannot concur, so Final Approval must come before signing; and confining the bidding to Chinese contractors violated the Filipino First policy, which is a positive command. Caguioa, J.: the conditions in the Approval-in-Principle were incorporated, so execution complied; the Filipino First policy does not reach localized projects. Gaerlan, J.: traces the borrowing power and its legislative, popular and administrative controls, and leaves open whether the approval-negotiation-approval framework itself complies. Lazaro-Javier, J.: voiding government acts for violating state policies needs adjudicative facts.

iss.q: Are the petitioners barred by res judicata or stare decisis (Bayan, 2000) from again assailing the VFA?
iss.why: The Court re-examined Art. XVIII, Sec. 25 on the merits and reaffirmed Bayan.

iss.q: Does the VFA violate Art. XVIII, Sec. 25: is the presence of US troops allowed “under a treaty duly concurred in by the Senate … and recognized as a treaty by the other contracting State”?
iss.why: The provision was meant to end the asymmetry of the old Bases Agreement. The Philippine Senate concurred in the VFA, and the US, through its authorized representative, recognized it as a treaty; that the US Senate did not give consent is a matter of US internal law (agreements are notified to Congress under the Case-Zablocki Act). Besides, the VFA implements the 1951 Mutual Defense Treaty, ratified by both Senates, under which the troops’ presence is allowed.

iss.q: Does the VFA’s custody clause (Art. V, par. 6) violate the Court’s rule-making power and equal protection?
iss.why: A foreign soldier admitted by agreement is substantially different from other accused. Under international law visiting forces are immune except as agreed, and the Constitution itself allows such arrangements (heads of State, diplomats, troops; Art. II, Sec. 2).

iss.q: Are the Romulo-Kenney Agreements, detaining the convicted Smith at the US Embassy, in accord with the VFA?
iss.why: The VFA separates custody during trial (Art. V, par. 6) from detention after conviction (par. 10), which must be in facilities agreed on and “by Philippine authorities.” An embassy room guarded by US personnel is not; the DFA must negotiate.

iss.q: (Resolution of February 3, 2009) Does Medellin v. Texas affect the VFA’s compliance with Sec. 25?
iss.why: The VFA is self-executing under Medellin’s own test and was actually carried out (the US produced Smith); it is implemented through the Case-Zablocki Act; the Mutual Defense Treaty received US Senate consent on March 20, 1952; and the framers required only recognition as a treaty, not a change in the other State’s domestic system.

nicolas.vote: 9–4. Azcuna, J. Dissenting: Puno, C.J. and Carpio, J., each joined by Austria-Martinez and Carpio-Morales, JJ. Nachura, J. (who had signed pleadings as Solicitor General) and Peralta, J. took no part.
nicolas.ops: Puno, C.J., dissenting: under Medellin, the VFA is a sole executive agreement that is not US domestic law; the “anomalous asymmetry” (the Philippines enforces it, the US cannot) means it is not “recognized as a treaty”; Smith should go to the New Bilibid Prison. Carpio, J., dissenting: Sec. 25 requires a treaty equally binding as domestic law in both States; notification under the Case-Zablocki Act is proof the US treats the VFA as a mere executive agreement; declare it unenforceable and transfer Smith.

iss.q: Is the President’s power to deport, and the Board’s power to investigate, limited to the grounds in Sec. 37 of the Immigration Law?
iss.why: There are two modes of deportation: by the President, after investigation, under Sec. 69 of the Revised Administrative Code, and by the Commissioner of Immigration under Sec. 37. Sec. 69 and EO 398 specify no grounds; deportation is an inherent power of the State, and the President, the sole judge of the facts, decides whether an alien is undesirable. Qua Chee Gan’s contrary remark was obiter. Possessing fake dollar checks and posing as a guerrilla unit are proper subjects of investigation.

iss.q: Is a prior criminal conviction needed, making the complaint premature?
iss.why: A deportation order does not depend on a judicial conviction (Ang Beng); even an acquittal of the same charge would not bar it. The Board only recommends; the President decides, and any abuse should be brought to the President first.

gotek.vote: Unanimous (Second Division). Aquino, J.; Antonio, J., concurring.
gotek.ops: Antonio, J., concurring: the law gives the Chief Executive full discretion to decide whether an alien’s residence is so undesirable as to injure the State, and a deportation order does not depend on a prior conviction.

iss.q: Were the petitioners denied due process when informations were filed while the prima facie finding was still under review?
iss.why: The Secretary of Justice and then the President affirmed the finding, so the claim lost its basis. Beltran filed a motion to declare the proceedings closed instead of counter-affidavits, waiving his chance; due process requires only the opportunity.

iss.q: Was Beltran’s right violated when the judge issued a warrant without personally examining the complainant and witnesses?
iss.why: Art. III, Sec. 2 stresses the judge’s personal responsibility to be satisfied of probable cause, not a duty to examine witnesses personally. The judge evaluates the fiscal’s report and supporting documents and issues the warrant, or, if not satisfied, requires affidavits of witnesses. Otherwise judges would drown in preliminary investigations.

iss.q: May the President initiate a criminal case by filing a complaint-affidavit?
iss.why: Immunity exists so the President can work free of hindrance or distraction. It belongs to the President by virtue of the office and may be invoked only by the holder, not by anyone else on the President’s behalf, so an accused cannot raise it. The President may waive it and submit to the court’s jurisdiction; the risk of perjury or contempt is the President’s own choice.

iss.q: Is Beltran not liable because the publication was privileged?
iss.why: The Supreme Court is not a trier of facts; it is a defense for the trial court.

iss.q: Would the prosecution have a chilling effect on press freedom?
iss.why: There was no basis to rule at that stage.

soliven.vote: 15–0. Per curiam; Gutierrez, Jr., J., concurring, reserving his vote on the chilling-effect issue.
soliven.ops: Gutierrez, Jr., J.: the Court should decide the chilling effect now, as in Salonga v. Cruz Paño: when a powerful President who heads the prosecution service sues a columnist, the publisher and editors in “a not too indubitable a case” for libel, the Court, not a lower tribunal, should draw the line (US v. Bustos; People v. Perfecto). Still, an incumbent President should not be left “bereft of legal remedies” against vilification.

iss.q: Was the petition for prohibition barred by presidential immunity, since it questioned an act the President approved?
iss.why: The petition was directed against the Secretary and the Regional Director, not the President, and the acts questioned were theirs; the CA’s injunction ran against them. Presidential decisions may in any case be questioned in court for grave abuse of discretion.

iss.q: Was prohibition improper because the petitioners were not acting as a court or beyond their jurisdiction?
iss.why: Grave abuse amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction was alleged, the petitioners themselves called the act ministerial, and courts may set aside administrative action that is capricious or arbitrary.

iss.q: Did the reassignment violate security of tenure?
iss.why: It was indefinite: the memorandum described him as fit for the post and set no period or purpose from which temporariness could be inferred. Security of tenure covers transfers without consent that amount to removal (Bentain); temporary transfers are allowed only if they are not a scheme to remove or force out.

iss.q: May the incumbent President be haled to court, even only for a petition for habeas data?
iss.why: Immunity traces to “the king can do no wrong”; the 1973 Constitution (as amended in 1981) wrote it in, and the 1987 Constitution left it out only because it was “understood in present jurisprudence” (Bernas). The lack of distinctions bars any: the President cannot be sued while in office. The US rule limiting immunity to official acts (Nixon v. Fitzgerald; Clinton v. Jones) is persuasive only, and Philippine immunity attaches for the whole tenure, whatever the subject matter. No balancing test applies; habeas data is covered, since granting it would find the President in breach of law; immunity need not be invoked (under Soliven, others cannot raise it for the President, but the Court applies it); OSG representation does not remove the distraction; and the petitioner is not without remedy: impeachment, or a suit after tenure.

iss.q: Were the President’s statements made in the discharge of official duties?
iss.why: Immunity applies whether the acts are personal or official.

iss.q: Was the petition wrongly filed with the Supreme Court under the Rule on the Writ of Habeas Data?
iss.why: The Court dismissed on immunity alone.

delima.vote: Bersamin, C.J., with Carpio, Peralta, Perlas-Bernabe, Gesmundo, Hernando, Carandang, Lazaro-Javier, Inting and Zalameda, JJ.; A.B. Reyes, Jr., J., separate concurring opinion; Leonen, J. (joined by Caguioa, J.), separate opinion. J.C. Reyes, Jr., J., on leave.

iss.q: Did the protest meet the requirement of specificity in alleging fraud and irregularities?
iss.why: The allegations were bare and generic, with no precincts named for Lanao del Sur and Maguindanao and only 11 of 422 for Basilan, and the annexes were defective; “mere doubts, fears” are not actionable (Peña v. HRET). The protest could have been dismissed outright but was heard for due process; the bar is higher for the two highest posts.

iss.q: Did the protestant show a reasonable recovery of votes after revision of the three pilot provinces?
iss.why: Under PET Rule 65, “not more than three” pilot provinces is a ceiling, chosen at the preliminary conference; no new rules can be made now. After revision, Robredo’s lead rose from 263,473 to 278,566, so the protest is dismissed without considering the other provinces.

iss.q: Does the failure of the recount bar the third cause of action, annulment of elections?
iss.a: YES; it fails on the merits anyway
iss.why: Rule 65 directs dismissal forthwith; Abayon is not precedent, and hearing the claim would need ad hoc rules. Even so, the Abayon requisites were not met: COMELEC rulings on the same failure-of-elections claims were final, the protestant did not allege that lawful and unlawful ballots could not be told apart or that Robredo was responsible, and annulling all three provinces still leaves her ahead by 15,130.

iss.q: Do the PET Rules allow different pilot provinces for each cause of action?
iss.why: The pilots cover all causes of action; otherwise more than three would be a fishing expedition.

iss.q: Does the ruling on the third cause of action affect the counter-protest?
iss.why: The counter-protest was dismissed in the dispositive portion.

iss.q: May the PET annul election results, and would that mean special elections?
iss.why: Annulment is an incident of the PET’s judicial function over a contested post; calling special elections belongs exclusively to the COMELEC.

iss.q: Did the PET incur inordinate delay, beyond RA 1793’s 20 months?
iss.why: RA 1793 was impliedly repealed when the PET became a constitutional body; the Constitution’s periods (Art. VIII, Secs. 13–14) do not fix one for it, and the case involved more than two million ballots.

robredo.vote: 15–0 to dismiss. Leonen, J., with Perlas-Bernabe, Gesmundo, Hernando, Carandang and Lazaro-Javier, JJ.; Caguioa, J., concurring separately. In the result: Peralta, C.J.; M.V. Lopez, J. (joined by Inting, Delos Santos, Rosario and J.Y. Lopez, JJ.); Gaerlan, J. (joined by Zalameda, J.).
robredo.ops: M.V. Lopez, J.: reasonable recovery should be measured by the share of protested precincts revised in the pilots; even so, Marcos failed. Gaerlan, J.: pushing the third cause of action would need new rules, best made through the PET’s rule-making power.

iss.q: Should the Court reconsider the finding of gross ignorance and the penalties?
iss.why: His arguments were rehashed and already refuted, and the penalties were milder than in similar cases. Spreading the decision on his record is official procedure. Blaming the fiscal for not citing the decree fails: courts must take judicial notice of all laws, so an avoidable error is gross ignorance, not a mere error of judgment.

iss.q: Was it irregular to keep the case with Justice Bidin after he moved from the Third to the Second Division, without notice?
iss.why: The case was validly raffled to him, and under the internal rules a case stays with its ponente when he changes divisions. No rule requires notice of such a transfer, which would reveal the ponente.

iss.q: Must every disciplinary case against a lower-court judge be decided by the Court en banc?
iss.why: Sec. 11 has two clauses: the first grants the power to the en banc and lets it set the procedure; the second requires the full Court only for dismissal. Regalado, J., who sat on the Commission’s judiciary committee, recalled that “en banc” was not meant to change the rule. Requiring the full Court for every reprimand would clog the docket and defeat the divisions of Sec. 4(1). A Division’s decision is the Court’s decision (Sec. 4(3); Circular No. 2-89).

gacott.vote: 14–0 (Regalado, J.; Narvasa, C.J., and 12 Justices concurred).

iss.q: Do the petitioners have standing?
iss.why: As people’s organizations and taxpayers raising a question of utmost constitutional importance, the citizenship of an appointee to the Supreme Court (citing Francisco and Tatad).

iss.q: Must the President be impleaded?
iss.why: The Executive Secretary is her alter ego and spoke for her. The suit does not stop the President from appointing; it targets the release of the appointment and Ong’s acceptance.

iss.q: Is the Court, not the JBC, the proper forum?
iss.why: Compliance with a constitutional mandate is of primordial importance, and the Court decides conflicting constitutional claims (Angara). The JBC has only initial competence over qualifications, which does not oust the Court.

iss.q: Is Ong natural-born and so qualified under Sec. 7(1)?
iss.why: The Court took judicial notice of his 1979 bar petition, in which he swore he was Filipino because his father was naturalized in 1964. BI and DOJ recognition cannot amend that final decision; a change of citizenship in the civil register is substantial and needs an adversarial Rule 108 proceeding, not RA 9048. His claim through his mother’s ancestry raises facts he must prove in court. Until then, accepting the post would violate the Constitution, so he was enjoined; the appointment was not annulled.

iss.q: Is a statutory arbitration with a final award binding a utility not party to the franchise valid?
iss.why: Courts favor arbitration unless it absolutely closes their doors. Parties may agree to arbitrate, but a franchise, a mere contract, cannot bind non-signatories to a final award; read literally, it leaves a public utility without any judicial determination of its dispute.

iss.q: May the members of the Supreme Court sit as a board of arbitrators under Sec. 11 of Act No. 1446?
iss.why: The Court faced a dilemma: as arbitrators the members would exercise either judicial power, apparently outside the Court’s jurisdiction and subject to review by the Court itself, or administrative power they cannot lawfully assume. The Court is one of three departments and exercises judicial power only; as guardian against usurpation by the others, it must keep strictly to its own sphere. Its jurisdiction is that of the Court acting as a court, not of its members as a board (citing Gordon v. United States).

iss.q: Are further proceedings needed?
iss.why: The material facts were more or less undisputed from the complaint and the answer.

iss.q: Was it dishonest to collect a judge’s salary without performing judicial functions?
iss.why: After his oath and assumption, he had a “perfect right” to the salary, especially when the offices bound to furnish his court failed to do so through no fault of his. He pressed officials for action and helped the DOJ in his spare time, which was to his credit.

iss.q: Is he liable for filing no reports and for incompetence?
iss.why: The Judiciary Act provisions and DOJ Circular No. 10 contemplate judges actually holding trials and deciding cases. He simply made himself available while the court could not open.

iss.q: May judges be detailed to, or assist, the Department of Justice?
iss.why: The Court does not look with favor at the long-standing practice, even if it concerns only the Secretary’s administrative authority over the courts. The line between what a judge may and may not do with the other departments must be “kept clear and jealously observed,” lest the separation of powers be eroded. No judge, even of the lowest court, should place himself where his actions may be reviewed, approved or reversed by anyone other than the Court of Appeals or the Supreme Court. No liability was imposed on him.

garciamacaraig.vote: 7–0 (Barredo, J.; Castro and Teehankee, JJ., took no part).

iss.q: May a sitting Justice be charged with disbarment?
iss.why: Members of the Court must be lawyers (Art. VIII, Sec. 7(1)) and are removable only by impeachment (Art. XI, Sec. 2). Disbarring a Justice would remove him by another route, circumventing impeachment. The rule covers the Ombudsman and his deputies, and members of the COMELEC and COA who must be lawyers. It protects judicial independence from charges by losing litigants and others.

iss.q: May a sitting Justice be charged criminally during incumbency?
iss.a: NO, if the penalty is removal
iss.why: Following Lecaroz v. Sandiganbayan, an impeachable officer may not be charged, while in office, with an offense carrying removal or a penalty whose service amounts to removal. The impeachment judgment is limited to removal and disqualification, and the convicted officer then faces prosecution (Art. XI, Sec. 3(7)).

iss.q: Is the rule an immunity from liability?
iss.why: It is a procedural requirement. The officer is not immune for crimes or ethical violations; he must first be removed by impeachment and then answers in the proper proceedings.

iss.q: May the Tanodbayan or a fiscal entertain charges against a Member of the Court?
iss.why: A prosecutor should forthwith and motu proprio dismiss such charges; one with a legitimate grievance should file an impeachment complaint.

ingonzalez.vote: 13–0 per curiam (Fernan, J., took no part; Gutierrez, Jr., J., absent).

iss.q: Can COA audit the Supreme Court?
iss.why: Art. IX-D, Sec. 2(1) lets COA audit government funds and property, on a post-audit basis for bodies with fiscal autonomy. That power must be read with the Court’s fiscal autonomy, the provisions on judicial independence, and the Court’s rulings on them.

iss.q: Is the in-house CFAG appraisal, not COA’s memorandum formula, valid?
iss.why: Judicial independence is decisional and institutional; its safeguards include Secs. 2, 3, 6, 10 and 11 of Art. VIII. Fiscal autonomy means “full flexibility to allocate and utilize” resources and freedom from outside control (Bengzon v. Drilon). The sale of property to retiring Justices is a retirement privilege under the Court’s administrative supervision, so the Chief Justice and the en banc decide its terms, including the formula. Under the Government Accounting and Auditing Manual, heads of offices have full and sole authority to dispose of property. COA’s substitution of its own policy would encroach on the Court’s autonomy.

iss.q: Did the exemption ever cover the sheriff’s actual travel expenses?
iss.why: “All court fees” means the legal fees under Rule 141 imposed as an incident of filing an action. A 2009 resolution already held that the sheriff’s actual travel expenses under Sec. 10 are neither court fees nor payable to the government.

iss.q: Can cooperatives still invoke RA 6938, as amended by RA 9520, for exemption from legal fees?
iss.why: In the GSIS resolution (2010), citing Echegaray, the Court held that the 1987 Constitution took away Congress’s power to repeal, alter or supplement the rules on pleading, practice and procedure; legal fees are a vital part of those rules. Fiscal autonomy also includes the power to levy and collect fees, which fund the JDF and SAJF, both meant to guarantee judicial independence; any exemption reduces them and is constitutionally infirm. Later rulings applied this to a cooperative and to NPC. The fallo does not expressly void Art. 61(6).

phcci.vote: 14–0 (Perez, J.; Del Castillo, J., on leave).

iss.q: Did the judge’s adding error change his vote so that Imperial won?
iss.why: His vote during and right after the contest ranked another contestant third and Imperial fourth; his calculations were not material. He had even raised the other contestant’s score to give her the edge.

iss.q: May courts reverse the award of the board of judges of an oratorical contest?
iss.why: For over 30 years, no one went to court over such awards; the board’s decision has been final by tradition and sportsmanship. A contestant has a privilege to compete, which becomes a demandable right only when proclaimed winner. The CFI assumed a wrong when there was at most an error; a wrong is the violation of a right, and Imperial had none. Any loss is damnum absque injuria. If fraud or malice were proven, the action would lie against the judge responsible. The ruling does not cover activities the government regulates through the Games and Amusements Board.

felipe.vote: 8–0 (Bengzon, J.; Feria, J., concurred in the result).

iss.q: Did the Court venture into “unwarranted factual inquiries”?
iss.why: Under Sec. 4(2), the Court en banc hears cases on the constitutionality, application or operation of regulations such as the circulars. Review begins with the police reports, but only to see whether they exist, were prepared as required and facially show compliance, not whether they are true: the Court is not a trier of facts. Its rule-making power over constitutional rights and the people’s right to information support the order. Relevance is for the Court to decide (Rule 128, Sec. 4), and David v. Arroyo itself struck down acts done under a valid proclamation.

iss.q: Are the documents covered by national security or state secrets?
iss.why: They concern routine police operations against illegal drugs; nothing shows that releasing them to the Court would prejudice sovereignty or foreign relations. It would be “simply ridiculous” that the Court could not read them while deciding the right to life of thousands.

iss.q: Did the OSG prove “legitimate operations,” or may it rely on the presumption of regularity?
iss.why: Bare allegations are not proof. The presumption does not apply because deaths are not supposed to happen in police operations, and it cannot override constitutional rights. If the OSG keeps refusing, the Court will presume the records adverse (Rule 131, Sec. 3(e)).

iss.q: Does the Amparo Rule bar the order?
iss.why: The point was not separately discussed; the order rests on the Court’s Art. VIII powers and Art. III, Sec. 7.

almora.vote: Unsigned en banc resolution (Sereno, C.J., on leave; Perlas-Bernabe and Reyes, Jr., JJ., on wellness leave).

iss.q: Must the Chief Justice and Justice Padilla inhibit?
iss.why: A motion to disqualify a Justice cannot be entertained after he has given his opinion on the merits; a litigant may not speculate on the result and object afterwards. The disbarment was a collective judgment, and Padilla’s former client was not a party.

iss.q: Did the decision need a Sec. 13 certification?
iss.why: The requirement refers to decisions in judicial, not administrative, cases; administrative matters are necessarily deliberated by the collegiate Court. Even if required, the signatures of the Members who took part attest to it, and a per curiam decision has no ponente.

iss.q: Did the minute resolution denying reconsideration violate Sec. 14?
iss.why: The requirement does not apply to an administrative case; in any event “lack of merit” is a statement of the legal basis.

iss.q: Is the CA decision void for lacking the Sec. 13 consultation certification?
iss.why: The first sentence of Sec. 13 restates the Court’s decision-making process since 1935; the 1973 Constitution extended it to lower collegiate courts, and the 1987 framers added the certification to ensure that decisions are made by the court as a body. Its absence does not mean the case was not reached in consultation; it shows only non-compliance and a basis to hold the responsible official accountable.

iss.q: Did the portions under the “voluntary right of way” become subdivision roads the Consings could not sell?
iss.why: The plan shows the right of way as the only access to the subdivision; the Consings admitted it was a road not included in the sale, yet the titles and contract included it.

iss.q: Is Santos entitled to a reduction of the price?
iss.why: Charging her for the road shifted to her the burden of providing access, which is unjust.

iss.q: Did the CA err in its computation?
iss.why: The price covered the house and lots as one property; splitting it in half was fair.

iss.q: Is there basis for attorney’s fees?
iss.why: The Consings acted in evident bad faith in constituting a so-called right of way over lots they sold.

iss.q: Are the Court’s deliberations and related records privileged against the impeachment court?
iss.why: Co-equal branches are exempt from each other’s compulsory processes as a matter of separation of powers and comity. The right to information is subject to limits provided by law; the Internal Rules keep raffle results, agenda actions and deliberations confidential. Predecisional and deliberative records are protected by the deliberative process privilege (Chavez v. PEA: deliberations of the Court or Congress cannot be pried open by a co-equal branch). Unauthorized disclosure is a crime the impeachment court cannot immunize. Justices cannot be compelled on internal matters but can be on external ones like bribery; the privilege extends to staff and belongs to the Court, not to any individual.

iss.q: May the prosecutors examine the four rollos?
iss.why: The rollos, pending or closed, contain privileged and confidential material; only certified copies of released issuances and pleadings may be given.

iss.q: Must the Clerk of Court produce the subpoenaed documents and testify?
iss.why: She may give certified copies of public records (petitions, released resolutions, the TRO, the bond receipt), which need no witness to authenticate; raffle records, logbooks and internal papers in pending cases stay confidential, and the Court would not waive the privilege for her testimony.

inreproduction.vote: Per curiam (Carpio, J., concurred with reservations; Sereno, J., concurred and dissented).
inreproduction.ops: Carpio, J.: the privilege covers only adjudicatory functions and yields to the express duty to explain a dissent (Sec. 13). Sereno, J.: the privilege is qualified and yields to impeachment; logbooks and administrative records are not deliberative; she would partly grant the request.

iss.q: Did the labor arbiter and the NLRC commit grave abuse of discretion?
iss.why: They held JCT and Cuevas liable without determining whether an employer-employee relationship existed or why Cuevas was solidarily liable, and computed the award from 1978 though JCT’s agreement began in 1989. The facts and law must be clearly and distinctly stated; parties must know how the case was decided so the loser can point out errors on review (Saballa). Failing to do so evades a constitutional duty. The case must be remanded to make the findings; remand, not dismissal, also favors the workers.

iss.q: Should the CA have denied the petition for failure to post the appeal bond and to move for reconsideration?
iss.why: The arbiter’s decision was a patent nullity, and the motion to reduce the ₱37.5 million bond was pending until 1996, so the bond rule was liberally applied. A motion for reconsideration is excused when the decision is a patent nullity. Individuals who did not sign the complaint must be dropped.

iss.q: Did the May 11, 1988 minute resolution violate Sec. 14, Art. VIII?
iss.why: It was not a “decision.” The requirement of facts and law applies only to cases submitted for decision, that is, given due course and briefed, not to an order refusing due course to a certiorari petition (Tayamura; Que v. People). The resolution also stated its legal basis. Certiorari is a prerogative writ, never demandable as of right.

iss.q: Is the municipality bound by the compromise its officials signed?
iss.why: The mayor, treasurer and provincial fiscal signed in their official capacity; the municipality is deemed impleaded and had its day in court.

iss.q: Did COA gravely abuse its discretion in disallowing the back salaries, leave and bonuses?
iss.why: They were paid under a binding, court-approved compromise.

iss.q: Did COA gravely abuse its discretion in denying separation pay?
iss.why: His separation was due to his dismissal, not the abolition of the post, and he had already received retirement benefits; double gratuity is not allowed.

iss.q: Did the trial court err in not stating the facts and the law on which its decision was based?
iss.why: It did not evaluate the evidence or discuss the legal questions, did not explain why it believed the complainant, why licking her genitals was attempted rape, or why it convicted on fewer counts than charged without acquitting on the rest; it even mismatched the counts and penalties. Sec. 14 (and Rule 120, Sec. 2) informs the parties of the reasons so they can appeal, and assures them the judge reasoned; it is a safeguard against ipse dixit.

iss.q: Is the accused guilty of rape?
iss.why: Inability to recall exact dates is minor in a child witness; delay was explained by fear of a father; his moral ascendancy substitutes for force; a medical examination is not indispensable. He was acquitted of the count whose date did not match, and the attempted rape became acts of lasciviousness.

iss.q: Was it reversible error to convict him of nine offenses in a single judgment?
iss.why: Unlike US v. Tanjuatco, the court rendered judgment on each of the nine informations; joint trial was without objection and allowed for a series of similar offenses.

iss.q: Did the CA fail to make complete findings on the last two errors?
iss.why: They were necessary consequences of the earlier errors.

iss.q: Did the CA violate Sec. 14 by quoting the Solicitor General’s facts?
iss.why: The Constitution requires only that the decision state the facts on which it is based; nothing forbids adopting the narration in the briefs, which exist to aid the court. The CA also made findings while discussing the errors.

iss.q: Did the CA deny reconsideration without legal basis?
iss.why: It found no cogent reason to reverse; that is the basis.

iss.q: Was the conviction unsupported by evidence; were the civil indemnity and the checks properly admitted; was the bank liable?
iss.why: One credible witness suffices; ownership is not an element of estafa; he who alleges forgery must prove it; the bank-negligence case he cited did not apply.

hernandez.vote: Vote not stated (Quiason, J., First Division).

iss.q: Should Yao’s appeal be dismissed for using the wrong mode of appeal?
iss.a: YES, but the Court reached the merits
iss.why: He filed a notice of appeal instead of a petition for review, on the last day; the right to appeal is statutory and the period is jurisdictional. But the Court ruled on the decision’s validity because it would grant him relief.

iss.q: Did the RTC decision comply with Sec. 14, Art. VIII?
iss.why: Memorandum decisions are allowed under BP 129, Sec. 40, but only under the Permskul conditions. The RTC merely quoted the MeTC’s dispositive portion and said it found no cogent reason to disturb it, without even summarizing the facts. It was “starkly hollow, otiosely written, vacuous in its content.” Faithful compliance with Sec. 14 is part of due process.

iss.q: Was Yao denied due process?
iss.why: Courts should give every litigant the amplest opportunity for a just disposition; the hollow decision denied him his day in court.

iss.q: Was certiorari under Rule 65 the proper remedy?
iss.why: Certiorari is “not a general utility tool in the legal workshop”; it corrects jurisdictional errors and is no substitute for an available appeal. It was treated as a Rule 45 petition.

iss.q: Are OCT Nos. 820 and 7477 valid?
iss.why: A Torrens title becomes incontrovertible after the period to question the decree; the original certificate is presumed valid, an earlier survey existed, and OCT 7477 was upheld in a 1955 case with the government. The residents also lacked standing: only the government may sue to revert public land.

iss.q: Was the CA decision void for not mentioning the 1906 survey?
iss.why: The CA reviewed and assessed the factual antecedents before applying the law. Not specifying a party’s contentions and the reasons for rejecting them does not violate the Constitution; denying a motion after deliberation, stating that the questions are factual or already passed upon, suffices.

iss.q: Were the Veneracions buyers and registrants in good faith, and so owners under Art. 1544?
iss.why: Good faith must attend both acquisition and registration. The first contract was an equitable mortgage. Before the real sale, they knew of Fr. Martinez’s possession and house yet relied on the seller, not even the owner, instead of asking him. The CA also erred: a sale of realty need only be in writing, not notarized.

iss.q: Is payment of the appellate docket fee within the period unnecessary to perfect an appeal from the MTC to the RTC?
iss.why: Under the 1983 Interim Rules, the fee is required but not a prerequisite to perfection; dismissal for non-payment is discretionary.

iss.q: Did the CA resolution denying reconsideration violate Sec. 14, Art. VIII?
iss.why: The CA said the motion posed nothing new and that its points had been considered and passed upon (Borromeo v. CA). That statement is the legal basis required.

iss.q: What is the period for the Sandiganbayan to decide?
iss.why: “Lower collegiate courts” in Sec. 15(1) refers to regular courts of that level, only the CA. The SB is a special court of the same level but with trial functions. PD 1606, Sec. 6 (unchanged by later amendments) and its own rules give three months from submission, without distinguishing original from appellate cases; the OCA’s split was rejected. A court cannot suspend its own rules or exempt a case. Motions for reconsideration and new trial: 30 days.

iss.q: Were cases undecided beyond the period?
iss.why: Some for over ten years. The reorganization, new justices and relocation were no excuse; one consolidated case is one case, not half the docket; unloading submitted cases to other divisions added to the backlog. “Justice delayed is justice denied.”

iss.q: Does Administrative Circular No. 10-94 (semestral docket inventory) apply to the SB?
iss.why: Given its purpose, to both original and appellate cases.

iss.q: Is the Presiding Justice administratively liable?
iss.why: Gross neglect and inefficiency: he is deemed ponente of unassigned cases; he had been warned before (Canson v. Garchitorena) and decided no case himself in a year.

delayssb.ops: De Leon, J., dissented on the period: the SB is a collegiate court with appellate jurisdiction at the CA’s level, so the Constitution’s 12 months governs over PD 1606.

iss.q: Is the judge liable for gross inefficiency for 70 late cases and 27 unresolved incidents?
iss.why: The Constitution requires trial judges to decide within 90 days from submission, and the New Code of Judicial Conduct requires reasonable promptness; the duty covers motions and incidents. A judge cannot choose his deadline; without an extension, even one late case is gross inefficiency (OCA v. Javellana). He sought extension only after the audit.

iss.q: Do travel, health and family reasons excuse the delay?
iss.why: He himself conceded no valid justification. The Court is sympathetic only to seasonably filed requests for extension.

iss.q: What is the proper penalty?
iss.why: Undue delay is punished by suspension without pay or a fine (Rule 140, Sec. 9(1)), depending on the number of cases, aggravating or mitigating circumstances, damage to parties, and the judge’s health and age. The separate complaint was absorbed to avoid penalizing him twice for the same omission.

iss.q: Does the petitioner have standing, and is he estopped?
iss.why: Except for the Biraogo argument, the motion raised nothing new, so the 2010 Decision stood.

iss.q: Is the PET unconstitutional because Art. VII, Sec. 4 does not expressly create it?
iss.why: The last paragraph grants the Court en banc the power to be the sole judge of the contests and to promulgate its rules, with no limitation on the method; the PET is a derivative of that grant. The framers (Davide, Regalado, Concepcion, Bernas) meant to constitutionalize the statutory PET of Roxas v. Lopez. By necessary implication, a grant of jurisdiction includes the means to exercise it; a power without means is a nullity (McCulloch).

iss.q: Is the PET a quasi-judicial body, so that the Justices in it violate Art. VIII, Sec. 12?
iss.why: Election contests are essentially judicial. The PET’s power derives from the Court’s judicial power; there is a “thin, but distinct line” between them, and the PET is independent but not separate from the Court. Sec. 4 of Art. VII itself authorizes it, just as Art. VI, Sec. 17 places Justices in the SET and HRET.

iss.q: Does Biraogo v. PTC require a law to create the PET?
iss.why: An “unmitigated quantum leap”: Biraogo found the Truth Commission justified under Sec. 17 of Art. VII, a differently worded provision on executive power, and the PET’s basis was expressly discussed by the framers.

iss.q: May the CSC try and decide an administrative case against a court employee, even one arising from a civil service exam anomaly?
iss.why: Art. VIII, Sec. 6 gives the Supreme Court administrative supervision over all courts and personnel: only it may oversee their compliance with all laws, rules and regulations. The CSC’s general disciplinary power and its power over exam anomalies (CSC v. Albao, a non-court employee) yield. The standard procedure is that the CSC files its complaint with the OCA (Ampong); it was ordered to refer the case.

iss.q: Was Andal estopped from questioning the CSC’s jurisdiction?
iss.why: Unlike the employee in Ampong, who admitted guilt and fully took part, Andal answered only because he was directed to, denied taking the exam, never appeared at the formal investigation, and raised lack of jurisdiction on appeal to the CSC.

andal.vote: 13–0, Carpio, J. Petition denied; the CSC to refer the case to the OCA. Guilt was not ruled on.

iss.q: Should Justices Leonen and Caguioa inhibit?
iss.why: There was no compulsory ground, and voluntary inhibition needs clear and convincing proof of extrajudicial bias. The resolution was an act of the Court en banc, a collegial body. His baseless bias claims were themselves direct contempt and a violation of Canon II, Sec. 14.

iss.q: Was the immediate preventive suspension, before his answer, proper?
iss.why: Disbarment is sui generis, an inquiry into fitness, unlike suspensions under RA 6770 or the civil service rules. The video spoke for itself, he admitted making it, and it had gone viral: waiting would have made the Court’s disciplinary power ineffective.

iss.q: Should Gadon be disbarred?
iss.why: Under the CPRA (applied to pending cases), a lawyer shall not behave scandalously in public or private life and shall not engage in gender-based harassment. The profane, misogynistic tirade aimed at a woman journalist violated both; “passion,” privacy and the victim’s reaction are no defense, since he meant her to see it. A prior suspension for emotional outbursts and many pending complaints aggravated it.

gadon.vote: 15–0, per curiam (June 27, 2023). Disbarred; ₱2,000 fine for direct contempt; immediately executory.
gadon.ops: None; Leonen and Caguioa, JJ., took part.

iss.q: May the Ombudsman entertain a criminal complaint against a judge for falsifying his certificates of service?
iss.why: Orap v. Sandiganbayan is not limited to offenses unrelated to official duty. One act may bring administrative liability to the Court (serious misconduct under Rule 140) and criminal liability under the Revised Penal Code.

iss.q: Must the Ombudsman first refer the complaint to the Supreme Court?
iss.why: Art. VIII, Sec. 6 gives the Court exclusive administrative supervision over all courts and personnel; an Ombudsman probe would encroach on it and on judicial independence. The Court holds the records, and the administrative question (whether a judge granted an extension must still report those cases) had to be settled first. Where a criminal complaint arises from administrative duties, the Ombudsman defers and refers.

macedavasquez.vote: 13–0, Nocon, J. Petition granted; the Ombudsman to dismiss the complaint and refer it to the Court.

iss.q: Did Justice Demetria intercede for the accused?
iss.why: The evidence was clear: he went to the DOJ with the accused’s ally and lawyer, asked the prosecutor to “do something to help,” and called the chief state prosecutor asking that the motion to inhibit be withdrawn. His alibi and denials did not hold against the prosecutors’ consistent accounts.

iss.q: Is he liable under Rule 2.04, Canon 2, and should he be dismissed?
iss.why: A judge must not influence a case pending elsewhere in any manner, and must avoid even the appearance of impropriety, as a private individual too. He need not know the accused; being the lawyer’s close friend and wielding influence is enough. His conduct undermined the integrity of the whole Judiciary.

inredemetria.vote: 14–0, per curiam. Dismissed, with forfeiture of benefits and disqualification from reappointment.

iss.q: Is Justice Roxas liable for grave misconduct, dishonesty and undue interest?
iss.why: He ignored a motion to inhibit him before issuing the TRO, left six motions unresolved, rushed the decision, and prepared a “transcript” of the deliberation from memory to support the Sec. 13 certification. Dishonesty is a serious offense warranting dismissal.

iss.q: Is Justice Sabio liable?
iss.why: By letting his brother, the PCGG Chairman, discuss the pending case with him, and by meeting a businessman about it, he failed the standard of independence and propriety, though he refused the ₱10 million offer.

iss.q: Are Justices Reyes and Dimaranan-Vidal liable?
iss.why: Reyes promulgated the decision without waiting for the Presiding Justice’s ruling on the chairmanship (simple misconduct, mitigated); Dimaranan-Vidal let herself be rushed to sign without reading the memoranda or deliberating (conduct unbecoming).

iss.q: Is Presiding Justice Vasquez liable?
iss.why: He failed to act promptly and decisively on the chairmanship dispute and let it escalate, damaging the Court of Appeals’ image.

revasquez.vote: Per curiam, September 9, 2008. Roxas dismissed; Sabio suspended two months; Reyes reprimanded; Dimaranan-Vidal admonished; Vasquez severely reprimanded.

iss.q: Did Justice Reyes’s retirement moot the administrative case?
iss.why: Retirement does not end administrative liability; disqualification and forfeiture of benefits can still be imposed, and public policy requires that last-days misconduct not go unpunished.

iss.q: Is Reyes liable for the leak of the unpromulgated ponencia?
iss.why: The leaked copy matched his office’s version (cover, page 1 and his initials on every page), not the copies of the other offices; his conduct was evasive and his staff contradicted him. Releasing an unpromulgated ponencia breaches the confidentiality of deliberations, and magistrates are held to a higher standard than clerks.

iss.q: May he be disciplined without a formal charge or direct evidence?
iss.why: Under res ipsa loquitur, once the facts are proven on the record and no credible explanation negates them, misconduct may be inferred without further hearing; circumstantial evidence may prove gross negligence and serious misconduct.

iss.q: May he be disciplined as a lawyer?
iss.why: In re Gonzalez bars disbarring an impeachable officer only during tenure; after retirement it is allowed with due process. The committee’s recommended indefinite suspension was modified to an order to show cause within ten days.

iss.q: Are his staff liable?
iss.why: Simple neglect: an unlocked drawer, an old page not shredded, no check on a case on hold. Fines of ₱10,000 and ₱5,000.

inrebiraogo.vote: 12–0, per curiam. Reyes fined ₱500,000 (from his retirement benefits) and disqualified from government office; two staff fined. Biraogo’s contempt was not ruled on.

iss.q: Does the Court have the power to change the venue or place of trial?
iss.why: Art. X, Sec. 5(4) of the 1973 Constitution expressly empowers the Court to order a change of venue or place of trial to avoid a miscarriage of justice. Here the accused’s personal safety was also at stake.

iss.q: Was Crisologo’s motion meritorious?
iss.why: Present hostile sentiment against the accused at the place of trial justifies a transfer; it would be absurd to compel him to stand trial where his life would be in danger. The fiscal agreed. A change of venue includes transferring the record to another court.

pilotin.vote: Aquino, J., Second Division (resolution, July 31, 1975). Motion granted.

iss.q: Should the trial be transferred from the CFI of Ifugao?
iss.why: The Court may change the venue to avoid a miscarriage of justice, though not for whimsical reasons, since crimes are best tried where committed. Serious and weighty reasons existed: the judge had been disqualified in another case as the Governor’s alleged political leader, and the accused’s life would be in danger in Lagawe. The case went to the Circuit Criminal Court in Baguio City.

iss.q: May private prosecutors file a petition for the People?
iss.why: The Solicitor General raised it but did not press it and adopted the petition; given the importance of the questions, the Court treated it as a certiorari petition.

iss.q: Should the venue be changed?
iss.why: The question is the effect of fear on the witnesses who will testify; doubts are resolved in favor of a transfer, and the plea could have been made administratively. A March 5, 1981 resolution had already moved the case to the CFI of Bacolod City and ordered protection for the witnesses.

iss.q: Was the grant of bail valid?
iss.why: In capital offenses, bail granted without giving the prosecution a chance to prove that the evidence of guilt is strong denies procedural due process and is void (People v. San Diego); the judge’s searching questions do not cure it.

sola.vote: 9–0, Fernando, C.J. (March 17, 1981). Petition granted; bail orders void.
